articles.title: Project Cargo East of Suez: Routing Oversized Freight When the Short Way Is Not Simple
articles.summary: Since late 2023, attacks on merchant shipping around the southern Red Sea have changed how many carriers route between Asia, the Red Sea, the Gulf and East Africa. articles.body: Since late 2023, attacks on merchant shipping around the southern Red Sea have changed how many carriers route between Asia, the Red Sea, the Gulf and East Africa. Much of the public discussion has focused on standard containers and headline freight rates. For shippers of project and oversized cargo, such as machinery, generators, steel structures and plant modules, the change has been more awkward. Their cargo depends on special equipment, careful planning and fewer options. This piece does not try to predict when conditions will change. It sets out the practical questions we now work through on every out-of-gauge file headed to these regions. Suez or the Cape: a decision made shipment by shipment For cargo moving between Asia and Europe or the Mediterranean, many carriers have chosen the Cape of Good Hope over the Suez Canal. That adds sailing time and changes port rotations. For cargo whose destination is itself on the Red Sea, such as Jeddah, Port Sudan, Aqaba or Hodeidah, sailing around the Cape is not the answer. The question becomes which carriers still call, how they call, and through which hub. This means routing decisions are made shipment by shipment rather than lane by lane. A routing that worked last quarter may not be offered now, and the same carrier may treat different destination ports differently. For oversized cargo, which often has a fixed site date and limited equipment, a quote should state the actual routing and carrier. A generic transit time is not enough. Hub switching and the extra handling it brings When direct calls are withdrawn, cargo is often moved through a transhipment hub and then a feeder or regional service. For standard boxes, that mostly means extra time. For project cargo, every extra lift is a risk. A flat rack carrying an over-width unit must be handled, stowed and lashed correctly at each terminal. Not every hub or feeder vessel is equally suited to out-of-gauge units. Before booking, we ask three things. Will the hub accept the unit’s dimensions and weight? Can the connecting vessel stow it on or under deck as needed? How long is the unit likely to wait for a connection? A switch of hub after booking can mean a new acceptance process, so it pays to confirm acceptance with the carrier for the full routing, not only the first leg. Flat racks and open tops: equipment is part of the plan Special equipment is not evenly distributed. Flat racks and open-top containers have to be positioned where the cargo is. When services change, empty special equipment can end up in the wrong place. Shippers should ask early whether the required equipment is available at the loading port for the intended sailing, and plan production around it. When out-of-gauge acceptance on container services is limited, breakbulk or a combination of containers and breakbulk becomes a real option. For some units, conventional vessels or multipurpose ships offer a more direct route to the destination than a container network that has been redesigned around the disruption. The right answer depends on dimensions, weight, destination port facilities and timing. War-risk insurance and surcharges Carriers may apply war-risk or emergency surcharges on affected lanes, and marine insurers may apply additional premiums for voyages through listed areas. These can change at short notice. Shippers should check three things. Does the freight quote include or exclude these surcharges? Does the cargo insurance policy cover the actual routing, including any listed areas? Who under the agreed Incoterm bears the cost if surcharges are introduced after booking? Agreeing this clearly in the sales contract avoids disputes later. Documents: small errors, large delays Rerouting and transhipment add places where documents can cause trouble. Bills of lading must reflect the actual port of discharge and any agreed place of delivery. For project cargo, packing lists should give accurate dimensions and weights for every piece, together with lifting points and centre-of-gravity details where relevant. Several destinations in the Red Sea, Gulf and East Africa have their own import documentation, pre-shipment certification or registration requirements. These should be confirmed with the consignee and destination agent before the cargo leaves origin, not after it arrives. What shippers can do now The common thread is to plan earlier and in more detail. In practice, that means: – Get routing and carrier details in writing for the specific destination port. – Confirm out-of-gauge acceptance for every leg, including the hub. – Check special equipment availability before fixing production dates. – Compare container and breakbulk options for oversized units. – Clarify war-risk surcharges and insurance cover against the actual routing. -Confirm destination document requirements before shipment. Conditions on these lanes may continue to shift, and I will not try to say how or when. What does not change is that project cargo rewards careful preparation. Shippers who ask these questions early keep more options open when routings move. About the author Delia Qu is Deputy General Manager at Dalian Yihang Shipping Agency Co., Ltd., a Class-1 international freight forwarder, NVOCC and AEO Advanced Certified customs broker in Dalian, China. She has more than ten years of experience in freight forwarding. Founded in 2020, the company handles ocean FCL and LCL, air freight, China–Europe rail, project and breakbulk cargo, and exhibition cargo to more than 80 countries through 180+ overseas agents.

Much of the public discussion has focused on standard containers and headline freight rates.

articles.title: Explainer: Why the US is trying to legitimize shadow fleet?
articles.summary: Washington wants to turn shadow-fleet tankers into legitimate ships. The capacity gain is small. The change to how sanctions work is not. Register The policy turn For two years Washington treated the shadow fleet as something to shrink. It designated tankers, seized a few and, in the spring, opened a licensed route to the scrapyard. On 19 October Energy Secretary Chris Wright described a different idea. Sanctioned tankers will be sold to approved investors, refurbished and put back to work carrying only non-sanctioned oil. In his words, ships move from the “bad-guy fleet” to the “good-guy fleet.” He insists nothing is being delisted, yet on 8 October OFAC removed two Iran-linked ships from its list after they were sold to US-aligned operators. Why now The motive is the Hormuz war. Since 28 February the strait has been effectively closed and tonnage has piled up around the Gulf. More than 40% of the world’s roughly 850 VLCCs sit in or near it. Moving crude to East Asia costs over six times its pre-war level and supertanker earnings touched a record of about $805,000 a day on 9 October. Attacks on tankers hit their highest weekly count of the war in early October. High freight makes US crude less competitive in Asia and feeds pump prices two weeks before the midterms. The capacity illusion Wright counts some 1,600 dark tankers, but few can be converted quickly. Analysts at Energy Aspects note that most ships sanctioned over Russian or Venezuelan links are already trading, so legalising them adds little real capacity. Many lack class certificates, most are over fifteen years old and licences can take months. The idle pool is mostly Iran-linked tonnage stranded by the blockade. Even so, freight futures fell and VLCC rates eased on the announcement alone. The market priced the signal before any ship changed hands. Washington is not lifting sanctions. It is turning them into a used-ship clearing house. A three-tier fleet A US licence does not clean a hull in Europe. Insurers in the International Group of P&I clubs are bound by EU and UK law, Britain keeps designating and can interdict ships in its waters, and France boarded a sanctioned tanker on 12 October. A converted ship may be legal in Washington and blacklisted in Brussels. That creates a middle tier between the compliant and shadow fleets, insured outside the mainstream and confined to US, Gulf and Asian trades. It is the first open split between the US and Europe on maritime sanctions since the price cap was built jointly. Who gains, who pays Sanctioned owners gain a profitable exit. Instead of a scrap price they sell at trading values close to an eighteen-year high, and that cash can buy younger hulls for the shadow trade. Mainstream owners, including EU fleets barred from buying EU-listed ships, watch the arbitrage go to others. Charterers, banks and ports must now check a ship’s status in two jurisdictions. The scrapping route loses its appeal, so old tonnage stays afloat in the most dangerous waters, where one casualty involving a “legitimised” tanker would carry heavy political cost. What it means The effect on freight will be modest. The effect on the industry will last. Rehabilitated hulls join a market whose orderbook is already about a fifth of the fleet, deepening the oversupply expected once Hormuz reopens. Most of all, the move turns sanctions from a fixed exclusion into a licensing market run from Washington.
takeaways: Washington wants to turn shadow-fleet tankers into legitimate ships.
The change to how sanctions work is not.

articles.title: Maersk schedules first India drydocking
articles.summary: Maersk will undertake its first planned drydocking in India, with the container vessel Maersk Chattogram scheduled to enter L&T Shipbuilding’s Kattupalli Shipyard near Chennai. The Singapore-flagged vessel is expected to arrive at the shipyard on 20 October 2026, subject to operational and weather conditions. The...
articles.body: Maersk will undertake its first planned drydocking in India, with the container vessel Maersk Chattogram scheduled to enter L&T Shipbuilding’s Kattupalli Shipyard near Chennai. The Singapore-flagged vessel is expected to arrive at the shipyard on 20 October 2026, subject to operational and weather conditions. The project represents the first operational milestone under the Memorandum of Understanding signed by Maersk and Larsen & Toubro during India Maritime Week 2025. The agreement established a framework for cooperation covering shipbuilding, vessel repair and the exchange of knowledge relating to international maritime standards and shipyard capabilities. Maersk Chattogram to undergo special survey The scheduled drydocking forms part of Maersk Chattogram’s normal lifecycle maintenance programme. Work will include the vessel’s special survey, together with inspection, maintenance and overhaul activities covering its hull, structure, machinery, equipment and propulsion systems. L&T Shipbuilding will use its Shiplift system at Kattupalli, described by the companies as the largest in India, to lift the vessel clear of the water. “The drydocking of Maersk Chattogram in India is a meaningful step towards turning our collaboration with L&T into action,” said Dinesh Kumar Balraj, Head of Fleet Operations East at Maersk. “We are aligning Maersk’s global technical requirements with India’s growing shipyard, supplier and maritime-service capabilities,” he added. Project brings together Indian maritime suppliers The project will involve Maersk’s fleet and technical teams, L&T personnel, Indian subcontractors, suppliers and maritime service providers. The partners will focus on safety, execution, quality and the exchange of operational knowledge during the drydocking. “The docking of Maersk Chattogram at Kattupalli advances our strategic partnership under the MoU and Framework Agreement signed between our organisations,” said Arun Ramchandani, Head of Precision Engineering & Systems at L&T. “Combining Maersk’s global maritime expertise with L&T’s shipbuilding capabilities, we aim to strengthen domestic capabilities and supply chains across the shipbuilding ecosystem,” he noted. The project moves the Maersk–L&T partnership from an exploratory framework to its first vessel-maintenance operation in India.

U.S. Coast Guard Photo The U.S. Coast Guard Cutter Munro has returned to its homeport in Alameda, California, following a 112-day patrol across the Bering Sea and Arctic Ocean that included monitoring Chinese research vessels, conducting joint exercises with Canadian forces and enforcing U.S. fisheries laws. The 418-foot national security cutter covered more than 23,000 nautical miles during the deployment, part of a broader effort to maintain a U.S. presence in the Arctic as Chinese and Russian activity draws increasing attention from Washington. Operating under the Coast Guard Arctic District, Munro monitored three Chinese-flagged research vessels operating in and around U.S. Arctic waters under Operation Frontier Sentinel, an ongoing effort to track foreign activity near Alaska and protect U.S. sovereign rights. The patrol included the July monitoring of the Chinese research ships Xue Long and Xue Long 2 , which transited north through the U.S. Exclusive Economic Zone and over the U.S. extended continental shelf in the Bering Sea. Foreign vessels are permitted to transit these waters under international law, but conducting marine scientific research within the U.S. EEZ or on its extended continental shelf requires prior U.S. authorization. The Coast Guard has said its monitoring operations are intended to ensure compliance with those rules and allow a rapid response to potentially unauthorized activity. The Coast Guard did not identify the third Chinese vessel monitored during the deployment in its latest announcement. Munro also conducted joint exercises with the Royal Canadian Navy, focusing on maritime law enforcement cooperation, maneuvering and improving awareness of vessel activity in Arctic waters. The cutter additionally participated in Operation Tundra Merlin, which brought together U.S. and Canadian military assets to test communications, command-and-control systems and coordinated responses to potential threats in northern maritime approaches. “The Arctic is a demanding maritime environment that can test any crew and vessel,” said Capt. Adam J. Disque, Munro ‘s commanding officer. “We also strengthened our enduring partnership with Canadian counterparts, advancing shared domain awareness and coordination across the remote region,” he added. Beyond its security mission, Munro conducted fisheries enforcement patrols in the Bering Sea, where boarding teams inspected commercial fishing vessels for compliance with federal safety regulations and fisheries laws. The Coast Guard described the mission as protecting Alaska’s commercial fishing industry, valued at approximately $6 billion. The deployment comes as the Coast Guard faces growing demands in the Arctic while operating with a limited number of ice-capable vessels. In September, the service confirmed to gCaptain that the medium icebreaker Healy would not complete its planned 2026 high-latitude mission following a significant engineering casualty in July. The breakdown left the Coast Guard relying more heavily on other assets, including the recently commissioned icebreaker Storis , national security cutters and aircraft, to maintain surveillance and patrol operations across the region. China’s growing Arctic presence has become a particular focus. Chinese research ships have conducted increasingly visible operations in northern waters, prompting U.S. and Canadian authorities to expand monitoring of their activities. The Coast Guard has emphasized that the presence of foreign research vessels is not itself a violation of international law, but says continued monitoring is necessary to protect U.S. interests in the region. Commissioned in 2017, Munro is one of four Legend-class national security cutters homeported in Alameda. The ship returned to Coast Guard Island on Friday following its nearly four-month deployment. articles.summary: The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers is overhauling how it manages dredging contracts nationwide, moving toward a centralized approach intended to reduce costs, improve scheduling and make better use of...

Stock Photo: Daniel Wright98/Shutterstock The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers is overhauling how it manages dredging contracts nationwide, moving toward a centralized approach intended to reduce costs, improve scheduling and make better use of the country’s limited dredging fleet. The Corps handles approximately 190 dredging contract actions each year to maintain navigation channels at U.S. ports, harbors and inland waterways. Most have traditionally been managed by individual districts, an approach the agency says can lead to duplicated administrative work, competing schedules and inefficient use of available dredging equipment. To address those problems, the Corps is establishing an Enterprise Dredging Delivery Center (EDDC), supported by an interim Dredging Evolution for Enterprise Production (DEEP) Team, to coordinate dredging requirements across the country. The goal is to treat dredging as a national program rather than a series of largely independent projects, allowing the Corps to coordinate contracts, schedules and equipment needs across multiple waterways. “For decades, we have approached dredging as a collection of individual projects—one district develops a contract, one gets awarded, and one dredge gets mobilized,” said Maj. Gen. Jason E. Kelly, while serving as the Corps’ deputy commanding general for civil and emergency operations. “While that model built today’s system, it is insufficient for the challenges we face tomorrow. The American taxpayer is not paying us to award contracts; they are paying us to maintain navigation channels.” Under the new approach, individual Corps districts will continue identifying dredging needs, handling engineering and environmental requirements, and coordinating with local ports and stakeholders. The centralized delivery center will provide contracting and planning support, with an emphasis on coordinating projects that compete for the same equipment and contractors. The changes could have significant implications for the U.S. dredging industry, where vessel availability, mobilization costs and project timing play major roles in determining how much work can be completed. By providing contractors with greater visibility into upcoming projects, the Corps hopes to reduce scheduling conflicts and give companies more certainty when planning vessel deployments, staffing and equipment investments. The agency has already begun testing new contracting approaches. In September, the Corps outlined plans to consolidate portions of its dredging workload into larger contracts and develop national procurement strategies. One initiative, called “Scope Dredge to Budget,” would allow contractors to compete on how much dredging they can accomplish within a predetermined budget, rather than simply bidding on a fixed quantity of material. The Corps held an industry meeting on October 16 to discuss applying the approach to navigation channels in Texas, including the Houston Ship Channel, Sabine-Neches Waterway and Corpus Christi Ship Channel. The broader restructuring is being introduced in phases, with the Corps previously identifying October 2027 as its target for establishing the permanent delivery center. The agency says it will continue consulting with dredging contractors and port stakeholders as the program develops, particularly to ensure that larger procurement packages do not undermine competition or disadvantage smaller and specialized operators. The initiative is part of the Army’s broader “Building Infrastructure, Not Paperwork” effort, which seeks to reduce administrative requirements and direct more resources toward infrastructure improvements. For the Corps, the ultimate measure of success will be whether the changes translate into more dredging and more reliable access to the nation’s ports and waterways. “The measure of success is not how many contracts we award; it is how many cubic yards we move,” Kelly said. “It is whether America’s navigation system is ready when the nation needs it.” Sign up for gCaptain’s newsletter and never miss an update Essential maritime and offshore news, insights, and updates delivered daily straight to your inbox Dive into a sea of curated content with our weekly ‘Dispatch’ email. articles.title: AD Ports Group reports reduction in emissions intensity in 2025
articles.summary: AD Ports Group has released its 2025 Sustainability Report, highlighting significant progress in its decarbonisation journey as the business continued its global expansion. Total emissions intensity, measured in tonnes of CO2 equivalent per AE$ 1 million in revenue across Scopes 1, 2 and 3, fell 6% to 190.68 tCO2e...
articles.body: AD Ports Group has released its 2025 Sustainability Report, highlighting significant progress in its decarbonisation journey as the business continued its global expansion. Total emissions intensity, measured in tonnes of CO2 equivalent per AE$ 1 million in revenue across Scopes 1, 2 and 3, fell 6% to 190.68 tCO2e from 203.06 tCO2e in 2024, demonstrating progress in decoupling emissions from business growth during a year in which Group revenue rose 20 percent to AED 20.77 billion. Total absolute emissions across the Group’s own activities and its full value chain rose 13% to 3,957,755 tCO2e, a rate less than the 20% revenue growth. The Maritime and Shipping Cluster, which generated 51% of Group revenue, accounted for 50% of Group emissions, followed by Ports at 24 percent, Logistics at 21% and Economic Cities and Free Zones at 5 percent. The Group also purchased 47,960 MWh of renewable energy certificates and diverted 10,303 tonnes of waste in 2025, a 24 percent increase on 2024. In 2025, AD Ports Group adopted a decarbonisation pathway covering its operations and value chain, with 139 initiatives planned between 2025 and 2050, aligned with the Paris Agreement’s 2°C goal and the UAE Net Zero 2050 strategic initiative. The pathway is backed by a projected USD 636 million investment over 25 years targeting a cumulative reduction of 2.9 million tCO2e. Specific 2025 initiatives included LNG-powered Pure Car and Truck Carrier vessels in the United Global Ro-Ro venture, ship-to-ship LNG bunkering and the launch of plans with Nimex Terminals to develop LNG and LPG terminal hubs at Khalifa Port. Executive compensation of senior management is linked in part to the achievement of sustainability targets. Captain Saif Al Mheiri, Abu Dhabi Maritime CEO and Group Chief Sustainability and Risk Officer, described defining a net zero pathway across a business of AD Ports Group’s scale as a significant achievement, expressing conviction that sustainable growth is achievable at scale through the embedding of decarbonisation into corporate strategy and decision-making.

The main support came from the bigger-size segment. The capesize index, which typically transports 150,000-ton cargoes, including iron ore and coal, also advanced for a second day, climbing 4.7% to 3,522 points. Meanwhile, the supramax index was steady at 1,868 points; and the panamax index, which usually carries 60,000 to 70,000 tons of coal or grain, fell by 1.7% to 2,247 points. articles.body: Shipping: More Newbuilding Contracting This Week in Hellenic Shipping News 21/10/2026 A number of newbuilding orders were reported over the past week. In its latest weekly report, shipbroker Banchero Costa commented that “newbuilding activity this week was broad-based, with significant contracting across the container, tanker, bulk carrier and gas carrier sectors. Chinese shipyards continued to secure a substantial share of the reported business, with Hengli Heavy Industries featuring prominently across several sectors. In the container sector, Zhonggu Shipping reportedly contracted 2x 14,000 teu containerships at Hudong-Zhonghua, priced at approximately USD 155 million each, with deliveries scheduled for December 2029. The vessels will feature conventional propulsion. A German owner was also reported to have contracted 4x 3,200 teu containerships at Hengli, priced at approximately USD 48 million each, with deliveries scheduled between June and December 2028”. Source: Banchero Costa The shipbroker added that “in the bulk carrier sector, Yangzijiang Maritime reportedly contracted 4+2 82,000 dwt bulk carriers at Jiangsu Watts & Engineering, with deliveries scheduled for March and June 2028. Eurodry also reportedly contracted 3x 82,000 dwt bulk carriers at Hengli Heavy Industries, priced at approximately USD 37 million each, with deliveries scheduled for September 2029. The owner had previously placed two further vessels of this type at the same yard in April and May 2026, although these contracts had not been made public. Tanker ordering was particularly notable this week. Liquimar Tankers reportedly contracted 3x 157,000 dwt crude oil tankers at Jiangsu New Hantong, with deliveries scheduled between June 2029 and June 2030. Top Ships reportedly contracted 4x 50,000 dwt tankers at Guangzhou Shipyard International, with deliveries scheduled for June 2029. The vessels will feature Ice Class 1A specifications. Emarat Maritime also reportedly contracted 5x 74,000 dwt tankers at Jiangsu Hantong Shipbuilding, priced at approximately USD 55 million each, with deliveries scheduled between June 2029 and December 2030”, Banchero Costa concluded. Meanwhile, in a separate note this week, Veson Nautical said that “bulker values held broadly stable this week, with Capesize edging slightly lower alongside softer earnings. The Capesize Pan Advance sold at a premium, in line with firm demand for prompt tonnage. Capesize Pan Advance (179,200 DWT, Sep 2009, Hyundai Heavy Industries Ulsan) sold to Greek buyers for USD 37.0 mil, VV Value USD 34.60 mil. Panamax Wei He (79,400 DWT, Jun 2012, Jinhai Intelligent Manufacturing) sold SS/DD due by Cinda Financial Leasing for USD 16.5 mil, VV Value USD 17.63 mil. Ultramax Bulk Guatemala (61,400 DWT, May 2013, Iwagi Zosen) sold to Lianson Fleet Group Berhad for USD 23.0 mil, VV Value USD 24.35 mil. Supramax Jin Xing (55,500 DWT, Jul 2007, Oshima) sold to Heng Fa Shipping for USD 14.6 mil, VV Value USD 14.12 mil. Supramax Shenli (56,000 DWT, Sep 2004, Mitsui Tamano) sold to Chinese buyers for USD 9.8 mil, VV Value USD 10.88 mil. Handysize Marem (34,100 DWT, Mar 2012, Dae Sun) sold SS/DD due by VG Shipmanagement for USD 13.0 mil, VV Value USD 13.40 mil. Handysize ZBB Serenity (37,300 DWT, Oct 2010, Huatai Heavy Industry) sold to Turkish buyers for USD 12.0 mil, VV Value USD 12.35 mil”. Veson also noted that “crude tanker values rose further as VLCC supply remained tight and buyers turned to Suezmaxes as a lower capital outlay alternative, with several 2010-built Suezmaxes reported at similar levels this week. Older tonnage also stayed in demand, with the 2004-built VLCC Southern Emperor changing hands. articles.body: New study finds shipping pays twice its share to EU ETS: earmarked revenues should triple to help build market for sustainable fuels and technologies in International Shipping News 21/10/2026 Shipping is responsible for around 10% of EU ETS emissions but pays almost 20% of the ETS bill. Unlike other sectors, it has never received free allowances. The new Sustainable Maritime Alternative Propulsion (SMAP) mechanism is a chance to reinvest part of this contribution in shipping’s energy transition. But a new study by European Shipowners | ECSA finds that the Commission’s proposed 110 million allowances cover only a third of what is needed. SMAP needs at least 330 million allowances (EUR 30 billion) to help create a market for sustainable maritime fuels and technologies, the study finds. For SMAP to meet this objective, this support must cover all sustainable fuels and technologies, including energy efficiency projects, that facilitate the energy transition of shipping. ES|ECSA calls on the European Parliament and the Council to at least triple the ETS revenues earmarked for SMAP. This is crucial to helping shipping meet FuelEU Maritime’s 2040 target, while helping to create a market for sustainable fuels and technologies that facilitate the energy transition of shipping. “Shipping pays almost 20% of the total ETS revenues, although it is responsible for 10% of the emissions covered by the ETS. Unlike other sectors, it has never received a single free allowance. The new ETS mechanism that earmarks part of these revenues offers an opportunity to support shipping’s energy transition. However, the Commission proposal covers only a third of what is needed to help create a market for clean fuels and tech. The European Parliament and the Council must at least triple the earmarked ETS revenues in SMAP to provide a credible market signal for the scale-up of sustainable maritime fuels and technologies, including energy efficiency projects. SMAP can contribute to the energy transition of shipping, but only if it is sized to match the scale of the challenge and covers all technologies that deliver carbon savings” said Sotiris Raptis, Secretary General of European Shipowners | ECSA. articles.title: Ports Are Scaling AI. Here’s How to Make It Deliver
articles.summary: Ports and terminals are no strangers to reinvention. Over the past 50 years, the industry has managed and adapted to the shift to containerization and ever-larger vessels, the move from paper manifests to electronic messaging and transactions, and the subsequent evolution to system-to-system integration with other...
articles.body: Ports Are Scaling AI. Here’s How to Make It Deliver in Port News 21/10/2026 Ports and terminals are no strangers to reinvention. Over the past 50 years, the industry has managed and adapted to the shift to containerization and ever-larger vessels, the move from paper manifests to electronic messaging and transactions, and the subsequent evolution to system-to-system integration with other parties in the shipping industries. But many port functions still run on clipboards, radio calls, or the gut instincts of a planner, who has watched the yard fill up and empty thousands of times. That is most visible at smaller terminals and in bulk ports. AI is the next wave, and this time it reaches the clipboard. It arrives as pressure builds from beyond the docks. The freight forwarders, logistics providers, and container liners that are a terminal’s customers are among the companies now investing heavily in AI, with spending across industries expected to increase over time. To assess how far the industry has come, BCG and TIC4.0 (an international nonprofit association of terminal operators and equipment and solution providers dedicated to the creation and promotion of digital standards for the cargo-handling industry) surveyed more than 100 leaders from across the container ports and terminals ecosystem. (See the sidebar, “Survey Demographics.”) AI is no longer an experiment at the edge of the business. On average, those we surveyed are already using or exploring the top 16 of the 43 use cases we assessed, from extracting data from shipping documents (62%) to predicting when a crane or straddle carrier will fail (48%). Survey Demographics In August 2026, BCG and the Terminal Industry Committee 4.0 (TIC4.0) surveyed the port and terminal ecosystem on the adoption of AI and generative AI, to establish where the industry sees the opportunity and where it sees the risk. Respondents were 103 experts across five continents, drawn from terminal operators, port authorities, container liners, and port vendors. They operate at regional, national, and global scale, and their companies are balanced across small (less than $1 billion in revenue), midsize ($1 billion to $8 billion), and large (more than $8 billion). The decision to adopt AI has been largely made across the industry. What it is worth has not been settled. The work now is to prove what it delivers, and to do it faster than the competition. Five findings from our survey show where the industry stands: • Adoption is broad, but proof is rare. Respondents are finding and testing use cases far faster than they are measuring what those use cases return, and only 4% can show a gain in earnings. • Unclear return on investment is the main barrier to accelerating implementation, and the doubt runs deeper the further you get from the C-suite. Other significant barriers are concerns about data quality and talent. • The demand comes from commercial customers, but the gains stay operational. Customers are asking for AI-enabled services, while respondents report keeping nearly all of the benefits inside their own operations. • The expected payoff is shifting from building AI to using it. Respondents expect the next three years of benefit to come from forecasting, dispatch, and workflow integration rather than from platforms and governance. • Investment is going into people and existing systems. That includes hiring and training AI talent, reskilling the current workforce, and adding AI to what is already installed. Together, those findings point to four moves: prove value before you scale, fix the foundations enterprise-wide, shift spending from setup to operations, and codevelop the commercial upside. Adoption Is Broad, but Proof Is Rare Nearly half (44%) of respondents have moved beyond early testing into scaling or a later stage, and size helps. Among the largest companies in the sample, those with more than $8 billion in revenue, 56% reported scaling or beyond, versus 32% of those below $1 billion. Activity, however, does not always create value. Only 11% of respondents track what AI contributes to efficiency or margin in any systematic way, and just 4% have embedded it in core operations and can point to a measurable gain in earnings. AI is at work inside the gate, in the yard, and in the back office, but almost nowhere is its contribution being measured. Unclear ROI Is the Main Challenge, and the Doubt Grows Beyond the C-Suite Unclear return on investment is the barrier named most often, cited by 41% of respondents. It sits well ahead of data quality at 32%, systems integration at 30%, and both executional certainty and implementation cost at 28% each. In short, what holds AI back is doubt about whether it will pay off. That doubt is not spread evenly and depends on where you sit. Only 21% of C-suite respondents named unclear ROI as a barrier, but below the C-suite, the figure jumped to 44%. The same divide shows up on cost, where just 14% of senior leaders pointed to implementation cost, versus 30% of everyone else. (See Exhibit 2.) C-suite enthusiasm has to be matched by a pragmatic implementation plan at the business-unit level, with full cost transparency for the managers who will be asked to deliver the result. This differentiated point of view on AI feasibility matters, as budgets are approved at the top, pilots are run below, and pilots scale only where the two agree. When the manager closest to the work still doubts the payoff, the test stalls. Yet C-suite respondents describe proven value at much the same rate as everyone else, 29% versus 26%. The open question is what counts as a credible business case. Standardized data quality is the second-most-cited barrier; roughly a third of respondents pointed to data quality and access as constraints. This comes as no surprise given that AI can only be as good as the information it runs on. The constraint is not only technical. Without shared definitions and semantics, AI can treat two measures that look comparable as if they mean the same thing when they do not and draw misleading conclusions from them. Today, much of that information still sits in fragmented, disconnected systems. Our 2025 digital benchmark with TIC4.0 saw the same problem from another angle. Most digital roadmaps are still drawn terminal by terminal, with no widely adopted standards, even inside the global and multinational groups that operate many terminals. The same benchmark found cybersecurity concerns slowing the adoption of advanced planning tools that reach across organizations, berth planning among them. In critical infrastructure, security and safety are part of the foundation rather than additions to it. Talent is another barrier. Roughly a quarter of respondents cited limited in-house expertise, with smaller shares naming resistance to change and a lack of training. The people who can run AI well remain thin on the ground. Neither barrier is a reason to wait. Both are reasons to build the foundation first, in the data that AI runs on and in the know-how of the people who will manage it. The Demand Is Commercial, but the Gains Stay Operational The pull comes from customers, not regulators. Asked which customers and partners are requesting AI-enabled services, respondents named freight forwarders most often (61%), followed by third-party logistics providers (58%) and container liners (52%), which likely reflects what their own customers, the cargo owners, expect of them. That tracks with the wider shift across logistics, where customers now pull adoption more than companies push it from inside. As forwarders and liners build AI into their own operations, they expect the terminal to keep pace. Respondents’ own reasons for adopting AI point the same way. Asked what motivated them, 69% named cost reduction and efficiency and 47% cited competitive pressure. Regulatory orders came last, at 1%. Port authorities do figure as a source of demand, named by 35%, but this shift is led by the market, not by compliance. Yet the value that respondents report is almost entirely operational. Operational efficiency leads the benefits realized or expected, at 74%, with faster decision making at 44% and cost reduction at 41%. A better customer experience reaches only 18%. (See Exhibit 3.) Customers are the stakeholders that are pulling hardest for AI, and the one benefit that would serve them directly is the one that is least reported. That 18% is open ground. Those that turn commercial demand into commercial value will pull ahead of those that keep every gain inside the fence. The Payoff Is Shifting from Building AI to Using It Asked where they expect AI to deliver the most benefit over the next three years, respondents pointed away from setting up AI and toward using it every day. Seven of the 43 use cases were residual “other” options and were excluded from this comparison. Of the remaining 36, respondents named 26 more often as areas of expected future benefit than as areas in use today, 4 were unchanged, and 6 were expected to decrease in relevance. (See Exhibit 4.) The biggest gains foreseen are in running the terminal. Forecasting operational states and their root causes rises from 49% today to 67% in expected benefit, and integrating AI into daily workflows climbs from 60% to 74%, the most-named use case for future value. Real-time equipment dispatch, predictive maintenance, and vision-based cargo safety monitoring advance alongside them. So do the two use cases that face the customer most directly: answering terminal status queries rises from 25% to 43%, and messaging freight forwarders from 39% to 55%. The industry may not yet be capturing the commercial upside, but it can see where the future lies. Our digital benchmark traced the same progression in the yard, where rule-based systems are giving way to predictive tools. Dwell-time forecasting estimates how long each container will sit before it moves, and smart stacking uses that estimate to decide where to place it, so the boxes leaving soonest are not under the ones staying longest. AI is carrying that progression into every corner of the operation. What recedes is the behind-the-scenes work. Internal governance falls from 51% to 37%, and internal platform building from 56% to 50%. Both still matter, but leaders increasingly treat them as groundwork. The window for winning on platform building alone is closing, and the advantage is shifting to operators that can embed AI in the workflows that move cargo. The Money Is Going into People and Existing Systems Investment is close to universal. Among the respondents to our survey, investment is close to universal with only 2% of respondents reporting no planned AI spending, though the sample leans toward large and global players, so investment is less likely universal across the industry as a whole. Hiring and training AI talent leads at 59%, followed by R&D budgets at 55% and adding AI modules to existing systems at 47%. The pattern is telling. Respondents are buying capability and building on what they already own, rather than replacing it. The workforce question runs deeper than any budget line. Half of respondents expect AI to reshape roles through reskilling or redeployment, 13% expect new roles requiring new skills, and 31% expect lower workforce demand as AI automates processes and decisions. Here, too, the view depends on seniority. Just 14% of C-suite respondents expect head count reduction, against 34% of respondents at other levels. That gap is a reason for leaders to say plainly what they intend. The automation in that 31% is AI automating processes and decisions, not the machines that move cargo. Equipment automation is a separate question. It replaces physical work at the ship’s side and in the yard, and our benchmark ranked it last among the digital capabilities it assessed, held back as much by labor agreements and community resistance as by capital cost. Those that lead the workforce shift with their people will move faster than those that manage it as a message. Four Moves Leaders Can Make BCG’s work on AI estimates that 10% of the value creation comes from algorithms, 20% from technology and data, and 70% from having the right training and processes in place. What this survey describes sits mostly in that 70%. These findings point to four moves, in two stages. The first stage answers the doubt about return and the gaps in data and skills, and it asks leaders to prove value before they scale and to fix the foundations enterprise-wide rather than terminal by terminal. The second stage follows the payoff to where operators and their customers can see it, shifting spending from setup to operations, and codeveloping the commercial upside with the customers already asking for it. The order matters, because an operator that cannot prove a use case pays, or cannot get at clean data, will not get far with the second stage. Prove value before you scale. With unclear returns the most-cited challenge, leaders should agree up front, for every pilot, on the baseline they are measuring against, the improvement they expect, the timeline they expect it in, and, above all, the single person who owns the outcome. They should agree, too, on what proven return will look like before the business case moves upward, since much of the gap between the C-suite and the frontline is a difference in definitions. Stage the rollout, with a go or no-go decision at each step, test the riskiest element first, and scale only once the value is shown. Evidence is what wins over a skeptical manager. Fix the foundations enterprise-wide. Data quality is the next barrier, so leaders should treat data as shared infrastructure rather than a series of local patches. Investing across the enterprise in data quality, access, and integration will unlock more value than any single use case, because piecemeal fixes tend to move the bottleneck rather than remove it. A port is a network of various stakeholders, such as authorities, terminals, liners, truckers, and depots, and data that stops at the terminal gate stops creating value there too. Common industry data standards are how systems learn to talk to one another. A quarter of respondents already plan to join industry collaborations or data-sharing initiatives over the next two years, and the shared semantics and data models that TIC4.0 is developing and promoting give that intent somewhere to land. Shift spending from setup to operations. Operators already expect the next three years of benefit to come from running the terminal. Put resources behind operational forecasting, workflow integration, and real-time dispatch, the areas with the clearest growth in expected benefit. Then back them with people. Say plainly what AI will mean for roles and fund the reskilling before the redeployment. Codevelop the commercial upside. The 18% customer experience figure is an invitation. Work directly with the forwarders, logistics providers, and liners that are already asking for AI and build the services they want, such as cargo visibility, proactive updates, faster documentation, and more reliable service. The industry has done this before. Since the mid-2000s, ports started to use vehicle-booking systems, sharply cutting truck turn times, and carriers proved willing to pay a booking fee for a guaranteed slot. Singapore has since applied the same idea on the water, with vessel slot booking. Ports such as Antwerp built data exchanges that they and their partners could turn into services. AI widens what can be offered and shortens the time it takes to offer it. The Next 12 Months Forty-four percent of respondents are at least scaling AI. Four percent can show what it delivers to earnings. Winners of the next phase will be those that can name a short list of use cases, built into core operations and measured against clear outcomes. That is a more modest ambition than the current wave of experimentation might suggest—and a far more valuable one, because connected value compounds while isolated value merely accumulates. For terminal leaders, those four moves reduce to three priorities: • Prove each use case on that short list against a baseline the operations manager closest to the work accepts. • At the same time, fund the data foundation as an enterprise-wide asset rather than a terminal-by-terminal project. • Once those two priorities have been addressed, move spending into operational AI and take what it enables to the customers already asking for it. In ports, technology has always served the business rather than set its direction, and the questions AI now raises about work and the workforce are not ones a technology function can answer. The hard part is discipline, in proving value, building the foundation, and choosing where to focus. That discipline belongs to the leadership team. articles.body: Secondhand VLCCs Now Valued Above Newbuildings in International Shipping News 21/10/2026 A t the end of September, a 15-year-old VLCC was valued above a newbuilding for the first time at USD 139.2 mil for 310,000 DWT, compared to USD 138.7 mil for newbuilding vessels. The move is part of a wider inversion of the age curve; a five-year-old VLCC is now valued 55% above a newbuilding (USD 218.0 mil against USD 140.6 mil), the widest gap on record and well ahead of the previous peak of 21% in December 2007. Newbuilding activity has reached remarkable levels The VLCC orderbook now stands at 38% of the fleet, more than double the 15% in 2025, and new tonnage set to hit the water is more sophisticated than the vessels it will join. Even so, newbuilding values are up only 12.4% year on year, from USD 125.27 mil to USD 140.8 mil, while a 15-year-old VLCC is valued up 196.35%, from USD 55.07 mil to USD 163.2 mil, according to VesselsValue data. The main driver is earnings. The situation in Hormuz has pushed spot earnings on the Middle East to China route to exceptional levels, and one-year timecharter rates are at a record high, more than tripling year on year. Older vessels give owners an immediate way to capture those earnings, and buyers are paying up for that. The impact on sales activity VLCC sales in the 15-to-20-year age category have risen 87.5% year on year, from 32 to 60 vessels over the same period. One notable sale is VLCC Eurospirit (320,100 DWT, Dec 2011, Daewoo) sold to Middle Easter buyers for USD 153 mil, VV value USD 165.75 mil. The vessel last changed hands in 2020 for USD 46 mil, so the seller has seen the value rise by USD 107 mil, up c.223%, more than tripling their initial investment. Buyers are concentrated with South Korea being the largest buyer this year, accounting for c.67% of all sales, driven by Sinokor’s large acquisition of VLCCs. The UAE is second place with 8%, followed by Greece with c.5%. Newbuilding is not a quick alternative. There have been 215 VLCC newbuilding orders placed this year, up 84% on the same point last year, but deliveries stretch into the 2030s. Anyone wanting to trade in the current market has to buy existing tonnage. With record earnings, an active sale and purchase market, and a long wait for new vessels, the demand for older tonnage looks set to continue. The key question is whether the 15-year-old premium over newbuilding holds if Hormuz-driven earnings ease. Source: Veson Nautical Tops 2026-10-21 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.title: MARPOWER Advances Key Technologies For Maritime Decarbonization
articles.summary: Maritime transport remains one of the most challenging sectors to decarbonize due to its high energy requirements, reliance on fossil fuels and the long operational lifetime of vessels. Against this backdrop, the EU-funded MARPOWER project (Efficient zero-emissions gas turbine POWER system for MARitime transport) is...
articles.body: MARPOWER Advances Key Technologies For Maritime Decarbonization in International Shipping News , Shipping: Emission Possible 21/10/2026 Maritime transport remains one of the most challenging sectors to decarbonize due to its high energy requirements, reliance on fossil fuels and the long operational lifetime of vessels. Against this backdrop, the EU-funded MARPOWER project (Efficient zero-emissions gas turbine POWER system for MARitime transport) is developing an advanced gas turbine-based energy conversion system for power generation and cogeneration on board ships, designed to operate with different sustainable fuels while improving overall efficiency. Two years into the project, the overall cycle and system design has been completed and detailed designs have been developed for its main components. Several critical technologies have also progressed into manufacturing and experimental testing, while the Digital Twin is becoming increasingly detailed. These advances range from optimised compressors and turbines and the successful testing of a combustion chamber prototype with 100% hydrogen to heat recovery technologies, active magnetic bearing systems and increasingly integrated digital models. Cargo container Ship, cargo maritime ship with contrail in the ocean ship carrying container and running for export concept technology freight shipping sea freight by Express Ship. top view Efficient operation of the MARPOWER system depends in part on the performance of its compressors and turbines. Designs for both the low- and highpressure compressors have now been completed, together with the aerodynamic and cooling design of the high-pressure turbine and the design and optimization of the low-pressure turbine. Their development has had to take into account several particular characteristics of the MARPOWER architecture. These include its two-shaft configuration, with both spools operating at the same angular speed, and the integration of active magnetic bearings (AMBs), which requires larger clearances to be considered in the aerodynamic design. Fuel flexibility adds another requirement, as operation with different fuels can result in variations in turbine inlet temperature. The work has also produced dedicated optimisation tools. For the high-pressure turbine, a new procedure was developed to optimise its internal cooling channels. The resulting design was assessed through advanced conjugate heat-transfer simulations and requires a coolant flow rate approximately 15% lower than estimates based on standard literature correlations. The low-pressure turbine has meanwhile been optimised using fully three-dimensional blade shapes tailored to its particular geometry. With the detailed three-dimensional configurations now available, further work will focus on characterising turbomachinery performance under off-design, transient and fuel-flexible operating conditions. Developing combustion for fuel flexibility Fuel flexibility is a central feature of the MARPOWER concept. The system is being developed to accommodate different sustainable and net-zero fuel options, including hydrogen, ammonia, renewable methanol and renewable methane, with limited modifications to the combustion system. The first MARPOWER combustion chamber prototype has been manufactured, instrumented and successfully tested with 100% hydrogen in an atmospheric test rig, following extensive Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) simulations and the build-up of the necessary hydrogen supply and distribution infrastructure. The experimental results, together with further simulations, are now supporting the design of a second prototype. This includes a flexible air distribution system and further geometry optimisations, intended to increase the fuel flexibility of the combustion system. Making greater use of available heat Improving the overall efficiency of MARPOWER depends not only on the performance of the gas turbine itself, but also on making greater use of thermal energy available within and downstream of the cycle. A scaled recuperator prototype has been manufactured and assembled and has passed nondestructive testing and pressure testing at 22.3 bar, around 22 times atmospheric pressure. The recuperator recovers heat within the gas turbine cycle. Its 1:100 capacityscale prototype incorporates a new heat-transfer surface geometry, while automated robotic laser welding has been implemented in its manufacture. Preparatory tests have been carried out and final modifications to the test facility are under way ahead of further experimental validation. The MARPOWER project combines recuperation with a complementary Waste Heat Recovery System to make further use of exhaust heat. The design of this system has been completed, covering the WHR boiler and the associated cycle, including the steam turbine, pump, generator, AMBs and rotor dynamics. Together, these approaches are intended to increase overall efficiency and reduce fuel consumption. Active magnetic bearings for high-speed machinery MARPOWER’s high-speed rotating machinery requires bearing and control technologies capable of supporting the rotor while limiting mechanical wear. Active magnetic bearings (AMBs) support the rotor without conventional mechanical contact and allow its position to be actively controlled, making them an important part of the MARPOWER energy conversion system. A new axial AMB has been designed, manufactured and integrated into an existing flywheel test rig, where initial rotor impact and recovery tests have been successfully conducted. A multiphysics mathematical model combining rotor dynamics, electromagnetics and the thermal behaviour of the AMBs has also been developed, providing a basis for future model-based control strategies that account for temperature-dependent effects. The project is also addressing the challenge of testing the 2.7 MW rotor system under ship movements. Similarity theory is being used to develop a smaller rotor reproducing the relevant dynamic characteristics of the full-scale system, together with a hydraulically actuated moving platform capable of reproducing surge, pitch and roll. This will allow rotor dynamics and AMB control to be investigated experimentally under representative movements at a manageable scale and compared with the full-scale system. In parallel, the high-pressure shaft prototype is progressing through mechanical design, Finite Element Analysis, rotor dynamics and AMB modelling, with work continuing towards manufacturing and subsequent experimental validation. Bringing the technologies together through a Digital Twin Understanding how the different MARPOWER technologies interact at system level requires their models and data to be brought together. A first calibrated version of the MARPOWER Digital Twin general model has been established around the selected system design point, with increasingly detailed component information being progressively incorporated. The simulation workflow has been automated to support systematic studies of different operating conditions, including part-load, non-nominal operation and fuel switching. A first system-level sensitivity analysis has also identified parameters with a significant influence on generated power and thermal efficiency, including turbine inlet temperature, ambient temperature and low-pressure compressor efficiency, helping prioritise subsequent parametric studies. A dedicated AMB sub-model has also been packaged as a Functional Mock-up Unit (FMU), allowing the rotor dynamics and thermodynamic models to exchange information and run together in co-simulation. As experimental data become available from the different technologies, they will progressively be used to refine and cross-validate the Digital Twin. Next steps: from individual technologies to maritime integration During the second half of the MARPOWER project, work will increasingly move towards further experimental testing, integration and validation under more representative conditions. Among the most immediate activities are further testing of the combustion chamber and recuperator, manufacture and assembly of the second combustion chamber prototype, further development and testing of the shaft and AMB configurations, and refinement of the Digital Twin using higher-fidelity component models and experimental data. The project is also entering the stage in which the complete energy conversion system will be assessed in the context of its integration on board ships. Two case studies will consider reference container and cruise vessels, examining basic engine-room arrangements and using digital simulations to assess energy and emissions performance under different operating scenarios. The vessel studies will also be relevant to the potential integration of MARPOWER technologies into existing ships. This is particularly important given the long operational lifetime of vessels and the technical and economic challenges involved in incorporating new technologies into the existing fleet. Technical performance alone will not determine the potential applicability of the MARPOWER system. Regulatory compliance activities will assess the proposed technologies against applicable safety regulations, standards and engineering practices, including consideration of an Approval in Principle (AiP) and a Technology Qualification Process (TQP), and support their progression towards future certification. Further work will address safety and risk, maintenance, Life Cycle Assessment and Life Cycle Costing. Together with the vessel studies and technical validation, these activities will provide a broader basis for assessing the integration, safety, environmental performance and economic implications of the complete MARPOWER system. Building on MARPOWER’s first two years The results generated during the first half of MARPOWER are also beginning to reach the wider scientific and engineering community. Technical advances from the project have already been presented at relevant international events, including ASME Turbo Expo and IFToMM Rotordynamics 2026. As experimental, modelling and validation activities progress, further results are expected to lead to scientific publications and new conference contributions. For Professor Jussi Sopanen, MARPOWER Project Coordinator at LUT University, the halfway point marks a transition towards a more integrated phase of the project: “During the first half of MARPOWER, we have advanced the system design, developed key technologies and started generating experimental results. The challenge now is to bring these developments progressively together, extend testing under more representative conditions and generate the evidence needed to assess the complete system and its integration on board ships”. The MARPOWER project brings together eleven partners from six European countries, combining complementary expertise across the technologies and disciplines required to develop and assess the proposed energy conversion system. Coordinated by LUT University, the consortium includes Aurelia Technologies, Alfa Laval, Politecnico di Milano, RINA Consulting, RINA Services, University of Vigo, the German Aerospace Center (DLR), the Technical University of Denmark (DTU), Chantiers de l’Atlantique and Zabala Innovation. The project will continue until August 2028. Source: MARPOWER 2026-10-21 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.title: Fund for Energy Efficiency Technologies (FEET) finances first two wind-assisted projects with Eastern Pacific Shipping
articles.summary: The Global Centre for Maritime Decarbonisation (GCMD), AIM Horizon Investments, and Eastern Pacific Shipping (EPS) today announced the financing for two wind-assisted propulsion systems (WAPS) projects through the Fund for Energy Efficiency Technologies (FEET), marking the fund’s first deployment. FEET is the world’s...
articles.body: Fund for Energy Efficiency Technologies (FEET) finances first two wind-assisted projects with Eastern Pacific Shipping in International Shipping News , Shipping: Emission Possible 21/10/2026 The Global Centre for Maritime Decarbonisation (GCMD), AIM Horizon Investments, and Eastern Pacific Shipping (EPS) today announced the financing for two wind-assisted propulsion systems (WAPS) projects through the Fund for Energy Efficiency Technologies (FEET), marking the fund’s first deployment. FEET is the world’s first fund to link verified fuel and regulatory savings from EETs installed on vessels to a pay-as-you-save mechanism. It offers up to 100% upfront financing through a blended finance structure. FEET is managed by AIM Horizon Investments, with GCMD as the fund’s decarbonisation advisor. It is also supported by the Development Bank of Japan, DBS Bank and ING. The fund’s first deployment finances the wind-assisted propulsion systems on board MV Pacific Sentinel and MV Pacific Sunstone. Each has installed three 22-metre suction sails on board, making them the first vessels in the EPS fleet to use WAPS. From left to right: Miki Akita, Managing Executive Officer, Development Bank of Japan Inc.; Max Lim, Managing Director & Group Head, Shipping, Aviation, Logistics & Transportation, DBS; Cyril Ducau, CEO, EPS; Lynn Loo, CEO, GCMD; Marcel de Bruijckere, CEO, AIM Horizon Investments; and Jens Van Yperzeele, MD, Transport & Logistics APAC, ING. From quantifying WAPS fuel savings to underpinning pay-as-you-save financing This deployment builds on an earlier collaboration between GCMD and EPS which led to the development of a methodology for quantifying fuel savings from the WAPS installed onboard the MV Pacific Sentinel. To isolate the retrofit’s impact from changes in operating conditions, GCMD collected 276 million data points over four months of spot-market trading in the Americas, from mid-May to mid-September 2025. From these, 203 valid on-off transitions were screened to quantify performance. Going forward, FEET will apply this methodology, reviewed by an independent third party, to determine fuel savings for the WAPS projects it finances. The project data will be audited, and the calculated fuel savings independently verified. These verified savings will then be used to determine payments from shipowners. Scaling EETs depends not just on proving that they work, but on establishing how much fuel they save under real-world operating conditions. With a methodology now in place to quantify those savings, FEET’s first projects with EPS take the next step: testing how pay-as-you-save financing works in practice, by linking payments to verified fuel savings. This is how we aim to turn operational evidence into investor confidence and unlock wider adoption of EETs across fleets. Professor Lynn Loo, CEO, GCMD Launching an innovative fund like FEET required a lot of effort, strong co-operation with GCMD and support by anchor investor Development Bank of Japan and debt providers ING and DBS Bank. The first deployment of FEET’s capital makes all that hard work worth it and delivers the proof of its concept. We learned a lot from our interaction with the finance and technical teams of EPS and look forward to applying those lessons when making our next investments and scaling up the fund. Marcel de Bruijckere, CEO, AIM Horizon Investments Decarbonisation moves faster when the technology, the data, and the financing come together. MV Pacific Sentinel has shown what wind-assisted propulsion can do in real operations, and we are pleased to now showcase this first FEET financing designed to assist shipowners wanting to invest in proven solutions. We look forward to seeing more energy efficient technologies make their way onto ships. Cyril Ducau, CEO, EPS Source: Global Centre for Maritime Decarbonisation (GCMD) 2026-10-21 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share
takeaways: FEET is the world’s first fund to link verified fuel and regulatory savings from EETs installed on vessels to a pay-as-you-save mechanism.
It offers up to 100% upfront financing through a blended finance structure.

articles.body: ENGINE: East of Suez Bunker Fuel Availability Outlook in International Shipping News 21/10/2026 Singapore and Malaysia Availability of all bunker grades in Singapore is very tight, with suppliers recommending a notice of 12-15 days for VLSFO, a source said. HSFO availability is expected to remain tight until November. Prompt availability for VLSFO and LSMGO is very tight at Malaysia’s Port Klang. East Asia Bunker operations at Zhoushan’s outer anchorages have been suspended since earlier today because of rough weather brought by Typhoon Champi, and disruptions are expected over the next few days, a source said. Availability remains strained despite low demand, with suppliers recommending lead times of around 11 days for VLSFO, LSMGO and HSFO. Supply conditions remain mixed across other Chinese ports. Suppliers are recommending lead times of 4-5 days for VLSFO, LSMGO and HSFO in Qingdao, Tianjin and Xiamen. In Nansha, VLSFO and LSMGO are available for delivery within 4-5 days. Suppliers in Shanghai and Ningbo are recommending lead times of 11 days for all grades. Bunker availability in Hong Kong is tight for VLSFO and HSFO and very tight for LSMGO, with suppliers recommending lead times of around seven days for good cover. Supply conditions are mixed across South Korean ports. Suppliers are recommending VLSFO lead times of 3-6 days at southern ports, including Busan, Ulsan, Masan, Onsan, Yeosu and Kwangyang. HSFO availability depends on stem size, delivery timing and other details of each enquiry. At western ports, including Incheon, Daesan, Dangjin, Pyeongtaek and Taean, VLSFO lead times can stretch to 15 days, while HSFO supplies remain limited. Japanese ports face severe supply constraints, as prolonged refinery maintenance and the prioritisation of domestic power generation limit the country’s bonded bunker fuel allocations. Available supply is fully committed to term nominations, leaving spot HSFO and VLSFO offers virtually unavailable. Occasional spot volumes emerge only when term cargoes are cancelled, according to a Japan-based trader. Refineries have yet to announce clear supply policies for November onwards, the trader said. VLSFO and HSFO availability is very tight at several Japanese ports, including Tokyo, Chiba, Kawasaki, Nagoya, Yokkaichi, Osaka, Kobe, Mizushima, Tokuyama and Oita. Kashima is also experiencing very tight availability of both grades. Oceania The approaching cyclone season, which runs from November to April, could disrupt bunker operations and fuel availability at ports in Australia, a source said. Weather remains the key operational risk for New Zealand’s bunker market. Wellington and ports across the South Island are particularly vulnerable to delivery delays when adverse weather disrupts marine operations. Middle East VLSFO and LSMGO availability is tight in Fujairah, while it is stable in Saudi Arabia’s Jeddah. VLSFO and LSMGO availability is tight in Oman’s Duqm, while HSFO supplies remain limited. Supplies of both VLSFO and LSMGO remain restricted at Qatar’s Ras Laffan. Further west, bunker inventories at Egypt’s Port Suez have fallen to critically low levels across all three major fuel grades. Djibouti is experiencing limited availability of VLSFO and LSMGO. Source: By Konica Bhatt, ENGINE, https://www.engine.online/news 2026-10-21 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.title: Antwerp-Bruges container throughput rebounds as empty volumes surge
articles.summary: The Port of Antwerp-Bruges recorded a strong recovery in container traffic during the third quarter of 2026, achieving its best quarterly performance since the final quarter of 2020. The improvement followed a difficult first half marked by weather disruptions, strikes and operational incidents. Total cargo...
articles.body: The Port of Antwerp-Bruges recorded a strong recovery in container traffic during the third quarter of 2026, achieving its best quarterly performance since the final quarter of 2020. The improvement followed a difficult first half marked by weather disruptions, strikes and operational incidents. Total cargo throughput reached 200.9 million tonnes in the first nine months of 2026, down 0.8% compared with the same period last year. Container volumes increased by 1.2% in TEUs, although container tonnage declined by 0.6%. Empty containers drive throughput growth The increase in container traffic was mainly driven by empty containers, which rose by 11.7% in TEUs. In contrast, full container volumes declined by 1.3%. According to the port authority, rising imports and weaker exports have increased the imbalance between inbound and outbound container flows. This has created greater demand for empty container repositioning, particularly towards Asia. Container operations also faced several disruptions earlier in the year. These included adverse weather, strikes and an oil spill in the Deurganck Dock. In July, a damaged container carrying hydrofluoric acid caused further disruption at the dock. Traffic began recovering in August, helping the port achieve its strongest quarterly container performance in nearly six years. “The strong recovery of container throughput in the third quarter shows the resilience of Port of Antwerp-Bruges,” said Rob Smeets, CEO of Port of Antwerp-Bruges. Middle East tensions reshape cargo flows Geopolitical developments have also affected the port’s trade patterns. Container exports to the Persian Gulf fell by 70%, while exports to other parts of the Middle East increased almost fivefold. The port authority said shipping lines had adjusted their schedules and introduced alternative routes to maintain connections with the region. Energy shipments were also affected. The port has received no LNG cargoes from Qatar since March, while diesel supplies from the Middle East stopped in mid-May. Other cargo segments recorded mixed results during the first nine months. RoRo throughput increased by 5.5%, supported by a 9.3% rise in new vehicle volumes, particularly from China and Japan. Dry bulk volumes grew by 13%, driven mainly by iron ore and other ores. However, conventional general cargo declined by 16.6%, with iron and steel volumes falling by 17.5%. Liquid bulk also remained under pressure amid weaker European industrial demand and high energy costs. Despite the recovery in container traffic, the port authority warned that trade barriers, geopolitical tensions and weak industrial activity continue to affect cargo flows.
takeaways: The Port of Antwerp-Bruges recorded a strong recovery in container traffic during the third quarter of 2026, achieving its best quarterly performance since the final quarter of 2020.
The improvement followed a difficult first half marked by weather disruptions, strikes and operational incidents.
Total cargo throughput reached 200.9 million tonnes in the first nine months of 2026, down 0.8% compared with the same period last year.

articles.title: HarborLab: Why shipping’s husbandry bills are still stuck in Excel
articles.summary: Shipping has spent years tightening voyage costs, bunker procurement and commercial port expenses, but one sizeable part of the bill remains comparatively untouched: husbandry. For Antonis Malaxianakis, founder and CEO of Athens-based port cost management platform HarborLab, that blind spot is particularly evident...
articles.body: Europe Maritime CEO Operations Tech HarborLab: Why shipping’s husbandry bills are still stuck in Excel Splash October 21, 2026 0 95 3 minutes read HarborLab HarborLab Shipping has spent years tightening voyage costs, bunker procurement and commercial port expenses, but one sizeable part of the bill remains comparatively untouched: husbandry. For Antonis Malaxianakis, founder and CEO of Athens-based port cost management platform HarborLab, that blind spot is particularly evident around bunkering, crew changes and stores, where technical departments can still be managing substantial sums through spreadsheets and email. “Husbandry calls have never carried the same profit and loss visibility as commercial port calls,” Malaxianakis tells Maritime CEO. The absence of cargo revenue against which expenditure can be measured has meant these calls have escaped some of the scrutiny applied elsewhere in ship operations. At the same time, the invoices are anything but simple. A port call can generate hundreds of pages involving port authorities, pilots, tug operators, customs brokers, bunker suppliers, repair companies and other parties. Pricing may vary even within the same port, while additional items such as demurrage, detention, congestion surcharges and equipment rental can emerge later. For Malaxianakis, who worked in disbursement departments at Thenamaris and Product Shipping & Trading before founding HarborLab in 2020, the problem is less about a lack of attention from technical managers than the tools available to them. The gap is particularly pronounced in Asia. “One data point from our analysis makes the structural difference concrete: 75% of technical managers in APAC still manage husbandry bills in Excel today, compared with 40% in EMEA,” he says. Across much of Asia, technical managers have direct control over dayto-day port expenditure but often lack a live reference against which an agent’s quote can be checked. HarborLab sees that combination as one reason APAC has become a priority market. “That combination, direct spending authority paired with heavier reliance on manual tools, does leave APAC more exposed to inconsistent pricing,” Malaxianakis explains.“The decision-maker already controls the budget; they’re simply working without the visibility to know whether what’s being paid is fair.” HarborLab argues that the difference between checking whether an invoice matches a quoted tariff and determining whether the quoted price was reasonable in the first place is where much of the potential saving sits. The company points to a controlled three-month trial with one customer in which half of a fleet remained on its existing disbursement account process while the other half moved to HarborLab. The HarborLab-managed vessels generated $220,000 in savings compared with $70,000 on the other half. “The gap isn’t down to one single lever, but the largest multiplier is benchmarking,” Malaxianakis says. “Manual review, however careful, can only check an invoice against a tariff document or a prior year’s DA; it can confirm a charge matches what was quoted, not whether the quote itself was fair.” HarborLab checks individual expense items against its database covering more than 1,400 ports. The system also picks up incorrect and duplicated charges, with the company then taking discrepancies back to agents in an effort to turn the finding into a credit. Benchmarking port calls is not as straightforward as comparing a bunker price or a standard commodity rate, however. Local tariffs, vessel types and individual port requirements mean two apparently similar services can legitimately carry very different costs. Malaxianakis argues that broad averages would therefore create another problem rather than solve the existing one. “Every benchmark is built at the level of port, vessel type, and expense category, not as one blended number, so a crane charge on an MR tanker at Tarragona is a different data point from the same charge on a bulker at Rotterdam,” he says. Behind that sits a database built from more than 40,000 port calls across over 1,400 ports. HarborLab says its analysts also obtain and verify official tariffs directly with ports rather than relying solely on historical invoices. Comparisons are then made against previously approved disbursement accounts for comparable ports and vessel types, while tariffs carry confidence indicators showing technical managers whether the underlying figure has been independently verified. “Local variation is built into the comparison rather than smoothed over,” Malaxianakis says. For a sector increasingly comfortable using data to scrutinise fuel consumption, vessel performance and voyage economics, his argument is that the same level of attention has yet to reach every invoice arriving from shore. And in husbandry, there is still plenty sitting in the spreadsheet.
