articles.title: Maersk reshapes Western Mediterranean–West Africa network
articles.summary: Maersk will launch a new WAF1 service and revise three existing West Africa services as part of an update to its Western Mediterranean network. The changes, scheduled to take effect from the third week of December 2026, will expand direct connections through Algeciras and Tangier to several West African markets. New...
articles.body: Maersk will launch a new WAF1 service and revise three existing West Africa services as part of an update to its Western Mediterranean network. The changes, scheduled to take effect from the third week of December 2026, will expand direct connections through Algeciras and Tangier to several West African markets. New WAF1 connection to Dakar The new WAF1 service will provide a dedicated connection between Algeciras, Tangier and Dakar. Its rotation will be: Algeciras – Tangier – Dakar – Algeciras According to Maersk, the service will improve connectivity to Dakar, including for cargo originating in Asia Pacific and the Middle East. The latest announcement does not clarify whether WAF1 will replace or operate alongside the previously announced WAF2 service, which was also scheduled to connect Algeciras, Tangier and Dakar. WAF5 expands Central West Africa coverage Maersk will also introduce a new Western Mediterranean rotation for WAF5, connecting Algeciras and Tangier with five West African ports. The WAF5 rotation will be: Algeciras – Tangier – Monrovia – Abidjan – Takoradi – San-Pedro – Lagos – Algeciras The carrier said the revised service would strengthen its coverage across Central West Africa and support important export cargo flows from the region. WAF3 and WAF6 receive additional calls The port coverage of WAF3 will be updated to include Tema, Onne and Pointe-Noire, providing direct connections between the Western Mediterranean and these markets. Meanwhile, WAF6 will be expanded with the addition of Cotonou. Maersk has not provided the complete revised rotations for WAF3 and WAF6 in its latest announcement. The network adjustments are expected to become effective from the third week of December in the Western Mediterranean. Maersk noted that the schedules remain subject to change.

articles.title: Gecko Robotics' USN Contract Expands to $300m
articles.summary: The U.S. Navy and General Services Administration (GSA) have increased the ceiling value of Gecko Robotics' maintenance and inspection contract to $300 million, more than quadrupling the original $71 million award just six months after its announcement.The expanded indefinite delivery…
articles.body: Gecko Robotics' USN Contract Expands to $300m Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 20, 2026 Image courtesy Gecko Robotics The U.S. Navy and General Services Administration (GSA) have increased the ceiling value of Gecko Robotics' maintenance and inspection contract to $300 million, more than quadrupling the original $71 million award just six months after its announcement. The expanded indefinite delivery, indefinite quantity (IDIQ) contract will support broader deployment of Gecko's robotic inspection and artificial intelligence technologies across the Navy fleet, with the objective of reducing maintenance costs and improving vessel availability. According to Gecko, its technology can identify structural problems up to 50 times faster than conventional inspection methods, reducing inspection periods from months to days and potentially saving up to $8 million in repair costs per ship. Central to the program is Gecko's Komodo robotic inspection system, which can scan through thick, non-skid deck coatings without removing them. The technology generates detailed corrosion and material thickness maps, allowing maintenance teams to identify structural deficiencies and plan repairs before vessels enter drydock. Gecko also deploys wall-climbing robots, drones and fixed sensors to inspect ship and submarine hulls, decks, welds and other structural components. Data is processed through its AI-powered Cantilever platform to assess structural condition and identify potential problems. "The conversation around AI and robotics in defense is no longer about experimental technology. It's about delivering measurable and impactful returns," said Jake Loosararian, Gecko Robotics co-founder and CEO. The contract expansion supports the Navy's broader effort to improve fleet readiness, including the Chief of Naval Operations' stated target of 80% readiness. The $300 million figure represents the contract's maximum potential value, rather than guaranteed spending. Image courtesy Gecko Robotics

articles.title: Shannon Foynesport reports record turnover
articles.summary: Shannon Foynes Port Company has reported a landmark financial performance for 2025, with turnover rising 12% to EUR 17.63 million and both EBITDA and operating profit reaching historic highs. EBITDA exceeded EUR 8 million for the first time, while operating profit reached EUR 5.71 million, up from EUR 4.81 million in...
articles.body: Shannon Foynes Port Company has reported a landmark financial performance for 2025, with turnover rising 12% to EUR 17.63 million and both EBITDA and operating profit reaching historic highs. EBITDA exceeded EUR 8 million for the first time, while operating profit reached EUR 5.71 million, up from EUR 4.81 million in 2024. Operating margin increased to 32.4% and EBITDA margin stood at 45.4%. Revenue growth was driven by robust performance across the port’s operations, with ship and cargo revenues increasing EUR 0.8 million or 10.1%. Total Shannon Estuary throughput rose 2.2% to 9.35 million tonnes, with Foynes Port recording its highest-ever annual tonnage, up 10.8% year-on-year. The company ended 2025 with a balance sheet value of EUR 71.6 million, net debt of EUR 6.9 million, a reduction of EUR 3 million on the previous year, and net assets of EUR 72 million, representing 240% growth over the preceding decade. Capital additions of EUR 4.59 million in the year related primarily to construction work in progress and the consenting process for the Foynes Island Deepwater development. The company’s Strategic Plan 2026-2030 identifies EUR 210 million in planned capital expenditure to develop port facilities and support long-term demand. Two significant connectivity milestones are approaching. The 40-kilometre Limerick to Foynes rail line is scheduled to reopen for freight services in the first quarter of 2027, representing a key enabler for sustainable logistics from Foynes and supporting Ireland’s Climate Action Plan modal shift objectives. The Adare bypass road project remains on schedule for completion by summer 2027, with financial appraisals underway for the Foynes sections and completion of the full scheme required by 2030 to comply with the TEN-T Regulation. CEO Pat Keating described the results as demonstrating the value of growing revenues, managing costs and maximising the capacity of the Foynes and Limerick terminals, while reaffirming commitment to the Vision 2041 priorities including offshore renewable energy infrastructure. Chairman Michael Walsh highlighted investment in Shannon Foynes as capable of unlocking significant societal benefits including job creation, carbon reduction and alternative fuel provision, with Ireland targeting 20GW of offshore renewable energy by 2040 and 37GW by 2050. He welcomed the launch of the National Designated Maritime Area Plan as an important milestone in providing clarity on future revenue streams for port developments including Foynes Island Deepwater Port.
takeaways: Shannon Foynes Port Company has reported a landmark financial performance for 2025, with turnover rising 12% to EUR 17.63 million and both EBITDA and operating profit reaching historic highs.
EBITDA exceeded EUR 8 million for the first time, while operating profit reached EUR 5.71 million, up from EUR 4.81 million in 2024.
Operating margin increased to 32.4% and EBITDA margin stood at 45.4%.

articles.title: Iran Claims More Tankers Hit Mines in Hormuz, But Evidence Remains Elusive
articles.summary: Iran’s Revolutionary Guards claimed Tuesday that a supertanker caught fire after striking a naval mine south of the Strait of Hormuz, adding to a series of similar claims that have...
articles.body: Advertise Forum Jobs Subscribe Grab a Seat at the Captain’s Table Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe. Join the leading maritime news network Vessels in the Strait of Hormuz, as seen from Musandam, Oman, July 31, 2026. REUTERS/Stringer Iran’s Revolutionary Guards claimed Tuesday that a supertanker caught fire after striking a naval mine south of the Strait of Hormuz, adding to a series of similar claims that have yet to be independently substantiated. The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy said the tanker was violating Iranian transit regulations when it struck a mine, according to Reuters. In another statement carried by Iranian media Tuesday , the Guards said two tankers had been set ablaze and disabled by mines along a route south of the strait that Tehran considers unauthorized. Neither statement identified the vessels or provided independently verifiable evidence of the reported strikes. The Guards also did not make clear when the two tankers were allegedly hit, leaving open whether the latest announcements describe new incidents or repeat earlier claims. The reports follow several similar announcements in recent months, many involving unnamed tankers said to have exploded or caught fire while attempting to use shipping routes not authorized by Iran. But assessments from the UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) and the Joint Maritime Information Center (JMIC) have repeatedly questioned those accounts. In its latest advisory, issued October 18 , JMIC directly addressed Iranian claims that two supertankers struck mines on October 17. “On 17 Oct the IRGC Navy claimed that two supertankers had struck mines in the Strait of Hormuz; there is no substantiation to these claims,” the advisory stated. The assessment, which covered developments through October 18, was issued before Tuesday’s latest statements. The October allegations are not isolated. On July 18, the IRGC claimed two oil tankers exploded and caught fire after entering a minefield in the southern Strait of Hormuz. The Guards accused U.S. intelligence agencies of encouraging the vessels to use the route but did not identify either ship. U.S. Central Command rejected the account as false. A similar claim followed on August 31, when Iranian state television reported that a supertanker had struck two naval mines, caught fire and come to a complete stop while attempting to use the southern passage. CENTCOM issued an unusually direct denial. “No ships have hit mines in the Strait of Hormuz,” the military command said, describing Iran’s announcement as an attempt to intimidate commercial shipping through disinformation. Just two days later, on September 2, the IRGC claimed another two tankers had exploded after striking mines. Again, the ships were not identified. The announcements continued in October. On October 10, Iranian authorities reported that a supertanker carrying approximately 2 million barrels of crude had struck a mine while using an unauthorized southern route. Two days later, the Guards described another incident involving a tanker reportedly carrying 750,000 barrels of crude, calling it a third mine strike. None of those announcements established the identities of the vessels or provided independent confirmation of the cause of the reported explosions. The clearest contradiction emerged last week following the sinking of the Singapore-flagged containership GFS Pride . Iran claimed on October 14 that a containership had struck a naval mine while using an unauthorized route. The description appeared to correspond with GFS Pride , which was attacked on October 13, caught fire and subsequently sank. But JMIC’s October 15 assessment identified the vessel as having been struck by an unknown projectile and explicitly stated that there was no substantiation for Iran’s mine claim. CENTCOM went further, identifying an IRGC projectile as the cause of the attack and saying the containership sank while being towed toward shore. All 21 crew members were safely evacuated. The ship’s sinking left containers and debris floating near the southern approaches to the strait. The lack of confirmation for Iran’s recent mine-strike claims does not mean the waterway is free of mines. In March, Reuters reported that Iran had deployed approximately a dozen naval mines in the strait, citing two sources familiar with the matter. U.S. forces subsequently carried out extensive mine-clearance operations. In late August, President Donald Trump announced that mines had been cleared from the strait’s international shipping lanes, a claim reinforced by CENTCOM commander Adm. Brad Cooper, who said U.S. forces had cleared the internationally recognized traffic separation scheme. However, the possibility of renewed mining remains a concern. JMIC’s October 18 advisory maintains a SEVERE threat level for the Strait of Hormuz and specifically warns mariners to remain vigilant for attempted mining within and adjacent to the traffic separation scheme. That assessment distinguishes a credible threat from a confirmed mine strike. The same advisory documented 153 confirmed maritime security incidents across the wider region since March 1, including attacks involving unidentified projectiles, drones and small boats. UKMTO recorded 12 attacks during the week covered by its October 16 overview. The latest reports include tanker attacks in the Arabian Gulf and a tug struck by two unknown projectiles near Khor Fakkan, UAE, on October 18. The advisory also reported that traffic through Hormuz remained approximately 70% below prewar levels, with 254 vessel transits recorded during the week ending October 14. Photo courtesy InterManager A new survey of more than 900 seafarers has exposed a persistent gap between safety procedures and the realities of working aboard ships, prompting renewed calls for action to prevent deaths in enclosed spaces. Ship management association InterManager says it has recorded 354 enclosed space accidents between 1996 and 2026, involving tankers, bulk carriers, containerships, passenger vessels and other ship types. Despite decades of safety campaigns, training requirements and regulatory attention, the association says many of the same problems continue to put seafarers at risk. The latest survey found that crews often struggle with overly complicated procedures, insufficient time and manpower, commercial pressure and inadequate practical training. Respondents also raised concerns that inspections sometimes place more emphasis on paperwork than whether safety measures actually work onboard. “Enclosed spaces have been killing seafarers for decades,” said Captain Kuba Szymanski, InterManager’s secretary general. “The industry does not need more paperwork for the sake of paperwork, it needs practical measures that work onboard.” “If a procedure cannot realistically be completed with the time, people and equipment available, then we need to question the system, not blame the seafarer.” InterManager says the findings point to a need for regular, practical training rather than relying on exercises completed early in a seafarer’s career. Crews should also have a greater say in developing the procedures and systems they are expected to follow. The association is calling for more frequent drills, refresher training, reliable gas detection equipment and effective rescue arrangements. It also sees opportunities to reduce risks through wearable gas monitors, digital entry permits, hands-free communications and remotely operated inspection equipment. Ship design is another concern. InterManager says better equipment placement, improved coatings and more durable piping could reduce the need for crews to enter potentially dangerous spaces in the first place. The findings come as the International Maritime Organization works to strengthen seafarer safety standards. In June 2025, the IMO adopted revised recommendations for entering enclosed spaces, addressing hazard identification, risk assessments and safe entry procedures. The organization is also conducting a broader review of the STCW Convention, with enclosed space training among the issues under consideration. International Maritime Organization +1 InterManager also criticized poor accident reporting and limited information sharing across the industry. The association warned that delayed or incomplete investigations make it harder for operators to learn from previous incidents and prevent similar accidents. “We already know many of the factors behind these accidents. What is missing is consistent action,” Szymanski said. “The priority now must be simpler procedures, better training, stronger leadership, improved ship design and far greater sharing of accident data.” InterManager will discuss the survey findings during a joint webinar with The Nautical Institute on October 27, bringing together maritime safety and human factors experts to examine what needs to change onboard and ashore. “Enclosed space deaths are not inevitable,” Szymanski said. “The industry has the knowledge to prevent them so why isn’t it doing it already?” Sign up for gCaptain’s newsletter and never miss an update Essential maritime and offshore news, insights, and updates delivered daily straight to your inbox Dive into a sea of curated content with our weekly ‘Dispatch’ email. October 20, 2026 © Sanmar Shipyards Sanmar Shipyards has delivered a new escort tug to the Greek joint venture SVS, comprising Vernicos Scafi, Spanopoulos and Lyboussakis, as part of its ongoing relationship with Med Tugs. Powered by two CAT 3516E main engines meeting IMO Tier Ill emissions standards, SVS Ill delivers a bollard pull of over 80 tons and achieves a free-running speed of 13.5 knots. The tug is also equipped with FiFi 1 firefighting capability, combining powerful performance with environmentally responsible operation. The RAstar 2900SX design has been developed to meet the demands of modern harbor towage and escort operations, providing the power, maneuverability and operational stability required to assist large commercial vessels safely and efficiently. SVS Ill joins the fleet operated by the Greek consortium, whose partners provide ship-handling and maritime safety services across Greek ports. Its arrival will support operations at Piraeus, one of the Mediterranean's major maritime hubs, while contributing to the consortium's efforts to strengthen its operational capabilities.

October 20, 2026 © Adobe Stock/Igor Kapustin Oil prices slipped after touching a five-month high during a choppy session on Tuesday as traders weighed Houthi attacks on Saudi infrastructure and reports of vessel attacks in the Gulf. Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis said on Monday they launched several attacks on Saudi energy, airport and military targets, such as an Aramco site in Yanbu, the Shaybah oilfield, Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport and Abha airport. Saudi authorities did not immediately confirm the Houthi claims and Reuters could not independently verify them. Brent crude futures fell $1.11, or 1.01%, to $108.44 at 11:36 a.m. ET (1536 GMT). That was down from the session high of $110.48, the highest since April for a nearby contract. The more active December contract was down 97 cents, or 0.98%, at $97.57 a barrel. "Oil prices remain well-supported. ... This suggests the market is pricing in a significant risk premium, given the situation's volatility," ING analysts said in a note on Tuesday. At least 18 vessels were reportedly attacked over two weeks, which keeps the risk premium intact, shiptracker Kpler said in a note on Monday. Also on Monday, a Houthi attack on a training camp for government security forces in Yemen's Shabwa province killed 58 people and injured more than 200. articles.body: Crowley has accepted delivery of Venture, a new chartered tug that will undertake ship-assist and escort operations at the ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach. The 82-foot vessel was built in the United States by Diversified Marine at its shipyard on the Columbia River. It is Jones Act compliant and purpose-built to assist large vessels operating within the San Pedro Bay port complex. Venture is powered by two Caterpillar 3516 engines compliant with US Environmental Protection Agency Tier IV requirements. The propulsion system generates more than 6,000 horsepower. Equipped with azimuth stern-drive thrusters, the tug can deliver up to 95 tonnes of bollard pull. Crowley said this combination provides the power and manoeuvrability required to assist some of the largest vessels calling at North American ports. Venture expands Crowley’s West Coast tug fleet “Venture strengthens our ship assist and escort capabilities in Los Angeles and Long Beach, providing the capacity and performance to help advance trade through this key corridor,” said John Ara, Vice President of Marine Services at Crowley. “Its advanced manoeuvrability and powerful engines allow us to meet the demands of some of the largest vessels calling on the West Coast, while supporting our commitment to safe, efficient harbour operations,” he added. Venture will join the Tier IV-compliant tugs Athena, Apollo, Hercules and Artemis in Crowley’s West Coast fleet. The ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach form the busiest container port complex in the United States. Escort tugs support the continuous movement, docking and departure of vessels carrying cargo through the gateway.

articles.title: Russian Diesel Cargoes Continue to Intended Destinations After Export Ban Lifts
articles.summary: Russian diesel cargoes are returning to their traditional destinations after the US suspended sanctions and secured the lifting of an export ban, with at least two tankers signalling trips to Turkey and Brazil in recent days, according to shipping data…
articles.body: Russian Diesel Cargoes Continue to Intended Destinations After Export Ban Lifts Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 20, 2026 © Adobe Stock/le Russian diesel cargoes are returning to their traditional destinations after the US suspended sanctions and secured the lifting of an export ban, with at least two tankers signalling trips to Turkey and Brazil in recent days, according to shipping data from Kpler and LSEG. Russia lifted its self-imposed ban on October 9 on diesel exports, introduced to tackle domestic shortages triggered by Ukrainian drone attacks on refineries, after striking a deal with US President Donald Trump to supply diesel to global markets. The deal included a temporary lifting of US sanctions on Russian fuel supply, though EU and UK embargoes on Russian fuel imports remain in force. Trump has set his sights on trying to calm diesel prices ahead of the midterm elections on November 3. Diesel is a key fuel used in industry, agriculture and transportation. Usually the world's second-largest exporter of diesel after the United States, Russia had already reduced its exports in summer before imposing the export ban. RUSSIAN DIESEL EXPORTS DOWN 41% THIS YEAR Total Russian diesel exports were around 345,000 bpd over this year so far, down 41% from last year, the data show. The tanker Leruo was signalling Manaus, Brazil, as its destination after departing from Russia's Baltic port of Primorsk on October 16, the data showed. The tanker Dolunay, which departed Primorsk with a diesel cargo on October 14, is heading for Alanya, Turkey. The two tankers are each carrying 300,000-barrel diesel cargoes, according to Kpler. Morocco has also begun importing Russian diesel since the lifting of the export ban. Turkey has received around 34% of Russian diesel loadings so far this year, Brazil 24% and Morocco 10%, according to Kpler data. ”With Russian supply returning, established trade routes are the most logical place for those barrels to go first. I would also expect Russia to prioritise customers that can absorb meaningful volumes quickly, rather than spend time developing new outlets when global diesel availability remains tight,” said Kpler’s head of geopolitical risk, Michelle Brouhard. Turkish fuel suppliers have reduced purchases of diesel from domestic refineries in anticipation of receiving Russian exports, three sources familiar with the matter told Reuters. Tupras and Socar, which operate Turkey’s major refineries, did not respond to a request for comment. RUSSIA SAYS IT COULD RAISE DIESEL EXPORTS SHARPLY Trump said Russia would immediately export 300,000 metric tons, or 2.25 million barrels, followed by 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons "immediately thereafter". Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said last week that Russian exports could surpass the levels agreed with Trump, aiming for up to 3.5 million tons per month (875,000 bpd) by the end of the year. The volumes Trump said Russia would supply are modest in comparison to the global shortfall, but at the levels Novak discussed, they would close most of the gap, Sparta Commodities analyst James Noel-Beswick said. Prices of European benchmark diesel futures LGOc1 have not changed significantly since the deal, according to LSEG data, and were trading at an $80 premium to Brent crude LCOc1 on Tuesday. This was off all-time highs of almost $95 in late September, but still several times higher than a year ago. Russian diesel loadings totalled around 210,000 tons, or 1.56 million barrels, over October 11-20, according to Kpler. (Reuters)

articles.summary: The European Union on Tuesday presented a new Arctic strategy reflecting the region’s importance to security, with pledges to boost satellite surveillance, increase monitoring of undersea cables and help EU members buy icebreakers.The Arctic is of growing interest to major powers including the US…
articles.body: European Union Unveils New Arctic Security Strategy Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 20, 2026 © Adobe Stock/Peter Hermes Furian The European Union on Tuesday presented a new Arctic strategy reflecting the region’s importance to security, with pledges to boost satellite surveillance, increase monitoring of undersea cables and help EU members buy icebreakers. The Arctic is of growing interest to major powers including the US, Russia, China and Europe, as melting ice opens up new shipping routes. US President Donald Trump tried to acquire Greenland, a territory of EU member Denmark, while friction has grown between Arctic nations and Russia since Moscow's 2022 invasion of Ukraine. "The Arctic is one place where the tectonic plates of geopolitics are colliding," said Ursula von der Leyen, the president of the European Commission, the EU's executive body. "When we see that sovereignty, territorial integrity, and the rules that have underpinned stability in the region can no longer be taken for granted, we have to act," she told reporters in Strasbourg. EU officials say Moscow has reopened and modernised Soviet-era military bases in the Arctic region in recent years and pointed out that Russia has a large concentration of nuclear weapons on the Kola Peninsula, inside the Arctic Circle. They say the Arctic has also become a testing ground for Russian missiles. Russia, for its part, has accused the NATO alliance of driving the region towards militarization. Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said in August that Russia sought to preserve peace and stability and reduce threats to national security in the region. EU PLANS TO BOOST PROTECTION OF SUBSEA CABLES Reflecting increased concerns about the safety of vital undersea cables and pipelines, the EU strategy says it will set up a " maritime security hub" to share information between EU members and partners from various sources "from seabed to space". As a first step, the EU plans to set up an Arctic cable hub to monitor, protect and help repair cables, according to the strategy, produced by the European Commission and EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas. The EU also aims to keep a closer eye on the Arctic as part of plans to expand its Copernicus satellite observation network. The 27-country bloc - which includes Arctic nations Finland, Sweden and Denmark - also needs more icebreakers, the strategy says. The new document - which did not put a price tag on its plans - is the first update to the EU's Arctic strategy since 2021 and the latest in a series of EU steps focusing on the region. Last month, von der Leyen unveiled plans for €200 million of EU investments in Greenland. (Reuters)

REUTERS/Ints Kalnins (Bloomberg) — A US plan to rehabilitate sanctioned tankers to boost oil supply may attract only a sliver of the dark fleet , as existing contracts, complex compliance checks and sky-high freight rates reduce incentives for would-be sellers. The measure — detailed on Monday, just weeks ahead of the US midterm elections — is the latest in a string of efforts by the Trump administration to cool crude and fuel prices driven higher by months of war in the Persian Gulf and the ongoing conflict between Russia and Ukraine. Soaring gasoline and diesel costs in particular have fueled affordability concerns among US voters. But with limited numbers of sanctioned supertankers actually available and would-be sellers unwilling to forgo lucrative crossings in the Middle East, industry analysts say the effort to revive so-called dark vessels may struggle to gain traction. “Sanctions relief does not equal immediately usable mainstream tanker capacity,” said Rahul Kapoor, global head of shipping analytics and research for S&P Global Energy. “The number of vessels that could realistically migrate back into mainstream trading would likely be materially smaller than the overall sanctioned fleet.” Under the US proposal, blacklisted vessels can be sold and rejoin the legitimate fleet, Energy Secretary Chris Wright said on Monday, adding the government would “convert” tankers to expand global availability but would not lift existing sanctions. He did not detail the sale process or potential investors. The US has previously removed vessels from its sanctions list if they met certain conditions. The supertanker Kiara M was blacklisted in December for supporting the Venezuelan oil trade, but was then deleted from the list in March after Washington moved Caracas’s oil trade to the mainstream. A wider plan would meet different hurdles — including the absence of financial incentives to sell up. Even though ships’ resale values have climbed in recent months, soaring freight rates mean that shipowners are still motivated to keep their vessels operating. A supertanker shuttling through the Strait of Hormuz can fetch as much as $40 million per trip, shipbrokers say. That compares to an early October price tag of about $190 million for a 10-year-old vessel, according to Clarksons data. There are also practical challenges, including the simple availability of vessels not already under contract, and the fact that the European Union and the United Kingdom not only also blacklist vessels but also dominate maritime insurance cover, potentially limiting unilateral efforts. Then there is age. Oil Brokerage, an independent energy broker, estimates that there are 294 sanctioned tankers free from EU or UK penalties — but 70% of them are above 20 years old and unpalatable to mainstream traders. That leaves just 75 commercially available tankers of all sizes, including 50 supertankers. “Any capacity return is likely to be gradual rather than immediate,” Oil Brokerage analyst Ting Jun Jie said. Fuel costs have been a pressing concern for the Trump administration, and efforts to cool oil prices over recent months have included periodic waivers on sanctioned oil and a diesel export deal with Russia. Brent remains near a five-month high, however, and a supercharged freight rally shows no signs of slowing. “The administration is doing all these things to bring down prices,” said Karnan Thirupathy, partner at Wotton Kearney who advises clients on sanctions compliance and other regulatory issues on global shipping. “It hadn’t been framed that way in the past. It’s an indication that they’re more inclined to do this more now than before.” © 2026 Bloomberg L.P. REUTERS/Mohammed Aty (Bloomberg) — Iranian attacks in the Persian Gulf are striking more ships and causing more severe damage than earlier in the conflict , bringing fresh risks to energy flows from the region. At least 23 incidents involving ships attacked in or near the Strait of Hormuz were logged in the first two weeks of October, with at least five reporting impacts to their engine rooms, according to data from naval groups in the region and alerts from security consultants. Direct hits on engine rooms can cause fires and leave ships without power or propulsion, taking vessels out of service for months and leading to costly repairs. Middle Eastern producers have shown a willingness to keep supplying oil in the face of Iranian attacks — preliminary data from trade intelligence company Kpler put the seven-day average of Middle East oil exports fractionally above prewar levels. But the intensifying strikes threaten to worsen one of the biggest constraints in the global oil market: the number of available ships. Several shipping and maritime security officials, speaking on condition of anonymity because of the sensitive nature of the topic, said they were seeing increased levels of engine-room damage from attacks, as well as a larger volume of incidents in general, but that it was hard to say if Iran was deliberately targeting ship engines. “What we’re seeing is an increase in the frequency of attacks, and therefore, more damage in engine rooms and disabling fire,” said Phillip Belcher, marine director at Intertanko, the world’s main trade group for the tanker industry. Persistent strikes on engines invoke memories of the 1980s Tanker War, when Iraq and Iran targeted oil tankers’ engine rooms in an effort to disable them. Some attacks caused fires and explosions that ultimately sank vessels. Dozens of damaged or sunken ships remained in the northern Gulf for years after. At least two recently-hit vessels sank last week, including a container ship that was struck in Hormuz. After the container ship sank, Pakistan’s Hydrographic Services said there were containers floating adrift near the United Arab Emirates. There were no attacks leading to engine damage in September, according to the data, and at least seven on non-Iranian vessels in previous months. When enforcing its blockade on Iranian ships, the US has also targeted engine rooms in order to disable vessels. Iran has recently begun using more missiles, rather than drones, to hit vessels, the shipping and maritime security officials said. Infrared-guided missiles tend to steer towards hotter parts of the ship, and often have larger explosive payloads than drones. For now, flows are continuing through the Strait of Hormuz, though estimates vary. US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said on Sunday that shipments are at about 80% of normal levels, and Iraq said Monday that its own exports are approaching prewar levels. But attacks on engine rooms will do little to draw owners back to Hormuz, and ships that come under attack remain out of action for longer as they undergo repairs. That could further restrict the number of tankers available to carry barrels, and push up the price of transporting energy. For a few days this month it was more expensive to hire a supertanker in some parts of the world than it was to send a rocket into space. “In a region where few owners are willing to put ships in, every VLCC hit is material,” analysts at Oil Brokerage Ltd. said in a note on Oct. 19, referring to very large crude carriers. Risks to the seafarers employed by shipping companies to sail through the region are also growing. One recent attack on a bulk commodity carrier struck the bridge and accommodation area where crew sleep, according to a report from the Joint Maritime Information Center, which distributes information on maritime security in the region. “Attacks often focus on the engine room or the bridge of the ships as it maximizes damage while keeping the risk of an oil spill relatively low,” said Jakob Larsen, chief safety and security officer at Bimco, the world’s largest shipping trade group. “Sadly, there are significant risks of crew injuries when these areas of the ship are hit.” © 2026 Bloomberg L.P. SPOT © CNES 2026, Distribution Airbus DS/Handout via REUTERS Maritime data provider Kpler has reached an agreement with Airbus to expand its ability to track vessels that disappear from conventional ship-tracking systems, adding daily satellite imagery to help identify ships operating without reliable Automatic Identification System (AIS) signals. The agreement, announced Tuesday , will integrate imagery from Airbus’s SPOT Earth observation satellites with Kpler’s existing vessel-tracking network, allowing analysts to detect ships independently of their reported AIS positions. The service will use high-resolution satellite imagery, with a resolution of 1.5 meters and a 60-kilometer swath, combined with artificial intelligence to identify vessels at sea and in port. The technology is intended to address a growing challenge for maritime tracking: determining whether a vessel has deliberately switched off or manipulated its AIS signal, or whether its reported position has been affected by interference with satellite navigation systems. That distinction has become increasingly important as AIS spoofing, GPS jamming and other forms of electronic interference complicate vessel tracking in major shipping corridors, particularly around conflict zones. While some vessels deliberately manipulate their positions to conceal movements, others may report inaccurate locations because of widespread Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) interference affecting multiple ships in the same area. By comparing AIS data with independently captured satellite imagery, Kpler says it can better distinguish between the two. “No single data source tells the whole story,” said Jean-Charles Gordon, Kpler’s vice president of maritime and logistics. Gordon said combining AIS information with satellite imagery and other independent sources would give shipping companies and governments a clearer picture of maritime activity, particularly when vessels disappear from electronic tracking systems. The expanded capability could also prove useful in monitoring sanctions evasion and so-called shadow fleet operations, where vessels sometimes manipulate or disable AIS transmissions to obscure their movements. In an earlier analysis of AIS spoofing and GNSS interference , Kpler identified the Persian Gulf and Strait of Hormuz, Black Sea, Baltic Sea and Red Sea among the maritime regions affected by navigation-signal interference. The company has also highlighted the importance of distinguishing deliberate AIS manipulation from external interference when assessing sanctions compliance and marine insurance risks. AIS remains the primary means of tracking commercial shipping, transmitting information including a vessel’s position, speed, course and destination. Kpler says its existing network collects billions of AIS messages daily. The Airbus partnership adds another source of information that does not depend on those transmissions, potentially allowing analysts to verify a vessel’s actual location even when its electronic track is missing or misleading. The companies did not disclose financial terms or specify when the expanded detection service would become fully operational. articles.summary: Iran has deliberately prolonged talks with the US to try to weaken Donald Trump politically ahead of November's US midterm elections, senior officials say, while fears of renewed military action and deep distrust of Washington have reinforced Tehran's reluctance to strike a quick deal to end the war.

Amirhosein Khorgooi/ISNA/via WANA (West Asia News Agency) via REUTERS DUBAI, Oct 20 (Reuters) – Iran has deliberately prolonged talks with the US to try to weaken Donald Trump politically ahead of November’s US midterm elections, senior officials say, while fears of renewed military action and deep distrust of Washington have reinforced Tehran’s reluctance to strike a quick deal to end the war . Three senior Iranian officials and an Iranian insider, speaking on condition of anonymity, said Tehran was convinced the US president was ready to resort to renewed attacks to try to break the stalemate in the eight-month-old war. “Iran is preparing for renewed Israeli and US attacks, not for a deal with America to end the war,” one of the officials said. “The clerical establishment is determined not to give Trump a political victory.” Tehran analyst Saeed Leylaz said that, by prolonging the talks, “Iran is influencing the US election without taking any unlawful action.” The war, which began in February when the US and its ally Israel launched strikes on Iran, has helped drive Trump’s approval rating to a record low as polls suggest that Americans worried about high gasoline prices will punish his Republican Party in the November 3 congressional elections. Trump has repeatedly said he expects oil prices to drop after the elections, but has not offered a detailed plan to end the war and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, a vital global energy shipping route effectively closed by Iran since the war began. Iranian attacks both threatened and real have kept ship traffic through the strait to a trickle, while a US maritime blockade and trade sanctions have cut off Iran’s oil export revenues and exacerbated growing domestic economic woes. With Tehran refusing to make concessions it believes could benefit Trump politically, there is little chance of a breakthrough before the elections, the officials said. Under pressure from Israel, Washington wants Iran’s decades-long nuclear program – which Iran says is purely peaceful and Western powers allege has military dimensions – on the table from the outset. For its part, Tehran insists that its conditions under a “seven-day plan” must be met before nuclear negotiations begin. And it offers no prospect of giving up the leverage over the Strait of Hormuz that the conflict prompted it to seize. Iran’s Foreign Ministry and the US White House did not respond to Reuters requests for comment. Iran’s proposal, conveyed through Qatari mediators, offered to reopen the strait within seven days, albeit under Iranian control, provided that Washington lifted its maritime blockade, eased restrictions on Iranian oil exports, released frozen assets and ended hostilities on all fronts. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said on Sunday that the offer remained on the table, with messages being exchanged through mediators. Tehran’s view that Washington cannot be trusted to commit to diplomacy stems from the attacks on Iran that have derailed previous negotiations, one Iranian official said. In June 2025, an Israeli attack wrecked plans for a sixth round of US-Iran nuclear talks in Oman. And last February, the US and Israel launched their war just after another round of talks ended, with further technical discussions scheduled. Maintaining a state somewhere between war and peace through the US midterms allows Iran to sustain pressure on Washington while reiterating its commitment to diplomacy. Trump has said the US will not bomb Iran again before November 3. However, the officials said Tehran continues to expect that bombing will resume, sooner or later. Alex Vatanka, director of the Iran program at the Middle East Institute in Washington, said the clerical establishment clearly wanted to hurt Trump politically. “But the fundamental issue is that Tehran believes that Trump is interested in regime change … and following Israeli Prime Minister (Benjamin) Netanyahu’s policy of seeking to bring down Iran’s ruling establishment,” he said. US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth discussed Iran with Netanyahu on Monday, three Israeli officials said, in an unannounced visit to Israel a week before a parliamentary election in which Netanyahu’s position is at risk. Iran’s strategy of keeping negotiations alive without rushing towards agreement comes at a cost. Prolonged uncertainty is weighing on Iran’s already crippled economy and wearing down public patience. Thousands were killed at the turn of the year when the security forces crushed spiraling anti-government protests. Annual inflation hit 73.6% in September, according to the Statistical Centre of Iran, and the rial currency has fallen nearly 35% against the dollar since Washington reapplied its naval blockade in July. Iran’s seaborne crude exports fell to zero in the second week of September from a 14-day average of 230,000 barrels per day at the start of the month, and remained there as of October 5, according to energy intelligence platform Vortexa. But the leadership’s distrust of Washington extends beyond the current conflict to existential concerns. Iran believes the US has repeatedly broken agreements even when Tehran honored its commitments, Leylaz said, leaving little confidence that any comprehensive deal would endure. “Reaching a sustainable deal with the US, even after the Trump administration, is no longer possible because of the deepened distrust,” Leylaz said. “Nothing will go back to the pre-war status quo.” (Writing by Parisa Hafezi; Additional reporting by Steve Holland in Washington; Editing by Kevin Liffey) (c) Copyright Thomson Reuters 2026. articles.body: Fairbanks Morse Defense Breaks Ground on New Center of Excellence Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 20, 2026 © Fairbanks Morse Defense Fairbanks Morse Defense (FMD) broke ground on a third Center of Excellence (CoE3) at the Bird-Johnson Propeller Company facility in Pascagoula, Miss. The new center will effectively double capacity to produce complex and powerful naval propulsion systems. The $60 million installation includes a $27 million U.S. Navy investment, $22 million of which is sourced from Australia’s initial contribution to the U.S. Submarine Industrial Base (SIB) under the AUKUS Pillar I effort. CoE3 will complement existing foundry capacity with the addition of 38,000 square feet of new manufacturing space, two new five-axis computer numerical control (CNC) machines equipped for parts weighing up to 100 metric tons (approximately 220,000 lbs.) and a machine-ready expansion slot for further growth. This capability will address current maritime industry capacity constraints and support submarine production and fleet readiness. The Pascagoula foundry upgrade will grow the workforce by 25%, employing a total of 100 highly skilled craftspeople. Once complete, CoE3 will support FMD training and apprenticeship programs and create new opportunities in high-tech manufacturing to strengthen the Gulf Coast economy and restore America’s defense industrial base. The addition of two new five-axis CNC machines with 7-meter turntables brings the total machine count to four. CoE3 also modernizes legacy foundry capabilities with a dedicated manufacturing bay for a future 3D sand printer. The current and future design establishes a versatile, fully integrated manufacturing hub that encompasses design and casting through machining, finishing and delivery. As the only privately-owned U.S. foundry certified for large-scale Navy propeller manufacturing, the Pascagoula facility is designated a U.S. National Asset. The center will be operated as a Bird-Johnson Propeller Company facility under the executive leadership of Fairbanks Morse Defense. FMD acquired Bird-Johnson in July 2025 and restored the Bird-Johnson name to the foundry, honoring the company’s nearly 70-year commitment to American-made naval propellers. The official groundbreaking coincides with America’s 250th anniversary, with new capacity scheduled to come online by Q1 2028.

articles.summary: The European Union unveiled a new Arctic strategy Tuesday aimed at strengthening maritime security, expanding icebreaker capacity and protecting critical infrastructure as melting sea ice opens new shipping routes and...

Join the leading maritime news network Photo courtesy European Commission The European Union unveiled a new Arctic strategy Tuesday aimed at strengthening maritime security, expanding icebreaker capacity and protecting critical infrastructure as melting sea ice opens new shipping routes and geopolitical competition intensifies across the region. The strategy , the EU’s first major update since 2021, marks a shift toward security and economic interests in a region increasingly important to global shipping, trade and energy supplies. At the center of the plan is a proposed Maritime Security Hub designed to improve surveillance and information sharing across the Arctic, including the monitoring and protection of critical undersea infrastructure. “The Arctic is one place where the tectonic plates of geopolitics are colliding,” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said Tuesday in Strasbourg. Von der Leyen pointed to Russia’s growing military presence in the Arctic, increasing pressure on regional security and the emergence of new shipping routes as reasons for Europe to take a more active role. “When we see Russia rebuilding its Arctic military footprint, pursuing hybrid strategies against the neighbors, and reshaping the security of the Arctic, it impacts the European Union as a whole,” she said. The new strategy comes as Russia, China, the United States and European countries compete for influence in the Arctic, where retreating sea ice is changing access to shipping lanes and natural resources. Maritime Security and Icebreakers Take Priority Under the plan, the EU will work with member states and Arctic partners to establish a Maritime Security Hub that brings together surveillance and monitoring information from satellites, vessels and seabed infrastructure. An Arctic Cable Hub would be an initial component, helping authorities monitor, protect and coordinate repairs to submarine cables across the North Atlantic and Arctic. The EU also plans to expand its use of satellite monitoring and data sharing, including a dedicated Arctic surveillance pilot scheduled for 2027 to improve maritime domain awareness. Icebreakers are another priority. The Commission said it will assess Europe’s shipbuilding capabilities and operational requirements while supporting joint procurement and resource sharing to increase the availability of advanced icebreakers. The effort reflects growing recognition that operating in the Arctic requires specialized vessels and infrastructure, even as sea ice retreats. Beyond security, the strategy calls for better integration of European ports, rail connections, energy terminals and digital infrastructure into emerging Arctic trade networks. The EU also wants to strengthen connectivity through a proposed Pan-Arctic submarine cable linking Greenland directly to Europe, with potential future extensions to Canada and Japan. Secure satellite communications would be supported by the EU’s IRIS² program, while a new ocean monitoring initiative known as OceanEye would improve data sharing, maritime safety and climate observations. A Changing Arctic Shipping Landscape The strategy comes as Arctic shipping draws increasing interest from governments and commercial operators seeking alternative connections between Europe and Asia. Russia has invested heavily in developing its Northern Sea Route along its Arctic coastline, while China has expanded its interest in polar shipping and infrastructure. For Europe, the changing Arctic presents both an economic opportunity and a security challenge. New shipping routes could create opportunities for ports, logistics providers and shipbuilders, but Arctic operations remain constrained by ice conditions, limited infrastructure, environmental risks and the availability of emergency response capabilities. The Commission said its approach will emphasize cooperation with Arctic partners, including Norway, Iceland, Canada, the United Kingdom and the United States, while complementing NATO’s role in regional security. The strategy also maintains the EU’s focus on climate change. The Arctic is warming nearly four times faster than the global average, according to the Commission, with consequences for sea ice, ecosystems and coastal communities. The EU reaffirmed its opposition to hydrocarbon development that threatens Arctic ecosystems, although the new strategy drops a previous commitment to pursue an international legal ban on new Arctic oil and gas development. Alongside security and economic development, the plan includes expanded polar research, investment in regional infrastructure and greater involvement of Arctic communities and Indigenous Peoples. More than half a million EU citizens live in Arctic regions of Denmark, Finland and Sweden. The Commission did not attach an overall price tag to the new strategy, leaving questions about how quickly some of the proposed security, shipping and infrastructure projects will move forward. Still, the new framework makes clear that Brussels increasingly views the Arctic not only as an environmental priority, but also as an important region for Europe’s maritime security, trade and economic interests. articles.body: Steerprop to Provide Ice-Class Propulsion for Danish Multi-Role Environmental Vessel Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 20, 2026 The new Multi-Role Environmental Vessel being built for the Royal Danish Navy by Karstensens Skibsværft will be equipped with two Steerprop SP 45 W azimuth propulsors and a Steerprop SP 10 TT tunnel thruster. Image: OSK Design. Finnish marine propulsion provider Steerprop has secured a contract with Karstensens Skibsværft to supply a complete ice-class propulsion package for a Multi-Role Environmental Vessel being built for the Royal Danish Navy. The vessel is one of four commissioned by the Danish Ministry of Defence Acquisition and Logistics Organisation to strengthen Denmark's marine environmental response and defense capabilities. The program is being delivered by Orlogsskibe Danmark, a consortium comprising OSK Design, Karstensens Skibsværft and Hvide Sande Shipyard. The project marks an important milestone for Steerprop, demonstrating the company's capability to deliver propulsion control systems compliant with DNV's SP2 cyber security requirements. Steerprop's will deliver two Steerprop SP 45 W azimuth propulsors rated at 2,200 kW each – including permanent-magnet motors also supplied by Steerpop - together with a Steerprop SP 10 TT tunnel thruster rated at 750 kW. The scope also includes bridge control systems and the complete propulsion control system. The integrated propulsion package is designed to support the vessel's DNV Ice Class 1A notation, enabling reliable operation in demanding ice conditions. Steerprop's W series azimuth propulsors combine advanced drivetrain design with highly efficient hydrodynamics to deliver reliable performance in some of the world's most demanding operating environments. The optimized housing geometry and robust cast-steel lower unit maximize efficiency, durability and operational reliability. The design has already proven itself in commercial applications ranging from harbour tugs to heavy-duty offshore vessels operating in demanding ice conditions. Steerprop has supplied mission-critical propulsion systems for governmental and naval vessel programs worldwide, including projects in Canada, the United States and across the Nordic and Baltic regions. Through these projects, the company has developed extensive expertise in meeting the demanding operational, technical and lifecycle requirements of naval and government operators. Construction of the vessel series has already begun at Karstensens Skibsværft's yard in Gdańsk, Poland. Steerprop will begin deliveries of the propulsion package in March 2027, with the first vessel expected to enter service in 2029.

articles.title: Maersk updates containerised vehicle booking requirements
articles.summary: Maersk has issued updated booking and acceptance requirements for vehicles transported in containers, following the introduction of dedicated UN numbers for battery-powered vehicles under IMDG Code Amendment 42-24. The requirements apply to new, used and damaged vehicles, including cars, motorbikes, e-bikes,...
articles.body: Maersk has issued updated booking and acceptance requirements for vehicles transported in containers, following the introduction of dedicated UN numbers for battery-powered vehicles under IMDG Code Amendment 42-24. The requirements apply to new, used and damaged vehicles, including cars, motorbikes, e-bikes, e-scooters, boats, forklifts, golf carts and aircraft. Whether a vehicle must be declared as dangerous goods depends on its power source and condition when it is handed over for transportation. Vehicle booking codes Customers must use the commodity code corresponding to the condition of the vehicle: Commodity code Description 004607 New vehicle, dangerous or non-dangerous goods 004608 Used vehicle, dangerous or non-dangerous goods 004609 Damaged vehicle, dangerous or non-dangerous goods Vehicles with unrepaired collision, structural, undercarriage or other material damage must be booked under commodity code 004609. Damaged electric vehicles may require an additional assessment before being accepted. Dangerous goods classifications The required UN number depends on the vehicle’s propulsion system: Vehicle type Classification Non-DG treatment under SP961 Petrol, diesel or gas powered UN 3166, Class 9 Permitted if all conditions are met Hybrid, including plug-in hybrid UN 3166, Class 9 Permitted if all conditions are met Fuel cell powered UN 3166, Class 9 Permitted if all conditions are met Lithium-ion battery powered UN 3556, Class 9 Must be declared as dangerous goods Lithium metal battery powered UN 3557, Class 9 Must be declared as dangerous goods Sodium-ion battery powered UN 3558, Class 9 Permitted if all conditions are met Other battery types, including lead-acid UN 3171, Class 9 Permitted if all conditions are met A vehicle may only be booked as non-dangerous goods when it satisfies every condition under Special Provision 961 of the IMDG Code. This includes having its fuel tank empty as defined by the Code. The forthcoming IMDG Code Amendment 43-26 will remove the current exemption available to hybrid vehicles. These vehicles will subsequently have to be declared as dangerous goods. The amendment may be applied voluntarily from January 2027 and will become mandatory in January 2028. Vehicles excluded from acceptance Maersk will not accept vehicles with damaged or defective batteries, flood or water damage, or signs or smells of leakage. Loose or spare batteries cannot be packed with a vehicle, although batteries installed in the vehicle are permitted. Vehicles are also prohibited from active reefer and non-operating reefer containers. Additionally, vehicles must not rest directly on or remain in contact with another vehicle inside the container. Loading and securing requirements The starter or auxiliary battery, normally the 12-volt battery, must be disconnected. Its terminals and cable ends must be insulated against short circuits. Vehicles must be switched off and cannot remain connected to a charger. Climate control, camping, security and other systems must also be deactivated. No cargo may be carried inside, on or attached to a vehicle. Standard equipment supplied by the manufacturer, including a spare wheel, jack and tool kit, may remain inside. Shippers are responsible for securing vehicles against movement in accordance with the IMO/ILO/UNECE Code of Practice for Packing of Cargo Transport Units. Maersk recommends that battery-electric and plug-in hybrid vehicles be transported with a state of charge of no more than 30%. Vehicles declared as dangerous goods should carry only enough fuel to enter and leave the container. The carrier also recommends placing dangerous goods placards on all four sides of containers carrying vehicles, as requirements currently vary between ports. The next IMDG amendment is expected to introduce a formal placarding requirement. Non-compliant bookings or containers may be rejected or held, with any resulting expenses charged to the shipper. Goods discovered inside vehicles will be treated as undeclared cargo.

MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Haeva Source: Petrodec Perenco UK, part of Anglo-French oil and gas player Perenco, alongside specialist contractor Petrodec, part of the Dixstone group, has undertaken a plug and abandonment (P&A) and infrastructure removal campaign in the Southern North Sea (SNS), which is seen as a step forward in the region's asset retirement activity. Perenco UK has confirmed the decommissioning of the Leman South (53/02a-15Y) and the Durango (48/21a-4z) subsea assets in the Southern North Sea, within a single campaign framework resulting in the plugging and abandonment of the wells and the removal of the associated subsea infrastructure. The company explains that these “highly complex” operations, which were completed in collaboration with Petrodec, were conducted safely and to the agreed timeframe using the contractor's Haeva jack-up vessel, building on recent experience gained from the Gawain , Arthur , and Davy subsea abandonment projects done using the same vessel. Jo White , Perenco UK SNS Managing Director, commented: “The Leman South and Durango campaigns were not routine P&A projects. They demonstrated Perenco's ability to deliver repeatable, large-scale, technically complex subsea well abandonment and infrastructure recovery using an innovative single campaign approach centred on Petrodec's Haeva, rather than relying exclusively on high-cost drilling rigs and standalone offshore projects. “I would like to thank our partners and the Perenco team who were involved in delivering some of the most technically demanding subsea well abandonment activities undertaken in the SNS.” This decommissioning milestone in the UK comes shortly after Perenco inked a gas deal for the Su Tu Trang Phase 2B project on Block 15-1 offshore Vietnam, set to supply more than 600 billion cubic feet (bcf) of gas over its life. articles.body: Asia Gas BW LPG India offloads 18-year-old VLGC for over $80m Adis Ajdin October 20, 2026 0 690 1 minute read BW LPG India BW LPG India New York- and Oslo-listed gas carrier giant BW LPG is cashing in again on strong secondhand values, agreeing to sell an 18-year-old VLGC for more than $80m as it presses ahead with a major fleet renewal programme. The company’s 52%-owned subsidiary, BW LPG India, has signed an agreement to sell the 2008-built, 84,601 cu m BW Loyalty for continued trading. BW LPG said the vessel had fetched a price in the low-$80m range, with the transaction expected to generate a gain of approximately $52m and net cash proceeds of around $66m after taxes and transaction costs. Both figures are calculated on a 100% ownership basis, rather than BW LPG’s attributable 52% stake in the Indian subsidiary. The ship will remain on its existing time charter before changing hands, with the sale expected to be completed by December. The buyer has not been disclosed. The latest disposal adds to a string of profitable sales by the Indian operation. In August, BW LPG India agreed to sell the 2007-built B W Birch , expecting approximately $64m in net cash proceeds and a $37m gain. That followed the July sale of another 2007-built VLGC, BW Elm , which generated around $64m in cash and a $36m book gain. Including BW Loyalty, the three announced transactions represent approximately $194m in net cash proceeds and $125m in gains on a 100% basis, although the latest sale has yet to close. The disposals come as BW LPG embarks on its largest newbuilding programme in years. In May, the company contracted eight 90,000 cu m panamax VLGCs at HD Hyundai Heavy Industries for approximately $940m, with deliveries scheduled between 2029 and 2030. The group subsequently raised $300m through a convertible bond offering in September, with the proceeds earmarked partly for financing the newbuilding programme. articles.body: Project & Tenders October 20, 2026 · 14 hours ago LNG Canada entrusts Técnicas Reunidas with €200M+ EPCM deal Técnicas Reunidas has secured work on LNG Canada's Coastal GasLink Phase 2, fueling the engineering firm's North American growth. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email LNG Canada Técnicas Reunidas, a Spanish-based engineering contractor, is cementing its footprint in North America, with an engineering, procurement and construction management (EPCM) assignment worth more than €200 million for Phase 2 of the Coastal GasLink pipeline awarded by LNG Canada, a joint venture featuring Shell, Petronas, PetroChina, Mitsubishi Corporation, and KOGAS. This four-year contract, which TR Canada E&C won for EPCM services related to Phase 2 of Coastal GasLink (CGL) in British Columbia on Canada’s west coast, deepens a partnership that began during the LNG Canada project's initial front-end engineering design (FEED) stages, marking another win for the Spanish engineering firm's North American growth strategy. CGL Phase 2 will be delivered through an integrated execution model, with LNG Canada leading project construction as Phase 2 Execution Manager and TR Canada E&C providing the EPCM services, while CGL will remain the owner, operator, and permit holder of the pipeline and associated facilities. The contract award comes only weeks after LNG Canada reached its Phase 2 final investment decision (FID) to advance the next stage of development of this British Columbia-based project of national significance. The project includes the construction of five additional compressor stations, as well as modifications to both existing and planned facilities at various points along the pipeline route. The newly awarded contract with LNG Canada adds to the company’s extensive experience in midstream projects, which includes 30,000 kilometers of oil and gas pipelines and more than 35 large compression projects worldwide. The award reinforces Técnicas Reunidas’ commitment to the North American market, a cornerstone of its current SALTA Strategic Plan. The firm has already identified a pipeline of potential projects worth €28 billion in the North American market. A significant portion consists of around a dozen large-scale combined-cycle power plants, primarily aimed at meeting the high and growing energy needs resulting from the boom in large data centers being developed in the region. REUTERS/Francis Malasig/Pool/File Photo By Liz Lee and Ben Blanchard BEIJING/TAIPEI, Oct 20 (Reuters) – China’s military said on Tuesday it had sent forces to watch a US warship that “illegally” entered waters around a disputed shoal in the South China Sea, while further north in the waterway, Taiwan reported a standoff with a Chinese vessel. China views almost all of the South China Sea as its own territory, despite overlapping claims by Brunei, Malaysia, the Philippines, Taiwan and Vietnam, with recent tension most pronounced between Beijing and Manila. The Chinese military’s Southern Theatre Command said the USS Charleston “illegally intruded” into waters adjacent to Sabina Shoal in the Spratly Islands without Chinese government approval in the early hours of Tuesday. “The US action infringes upon China’s sovereign rights and interests, jeopardizes maritime security, and is detrimental to regional peace and stability,” it said in a statement. “The US side should immediately cease such activities.” China’s navy dispatched forces to track and monitor the ship, it added. The US Navy did not immediately respond to a request for comment. It generally refers to such missions as “freedom of navigation operations,” though its last known one in the South China Sea was more than a year ago. A Philippines’ military spokesperson said the US ship “did not trespass into ‘Chinese territory’,” adding that no nation had the authority to require prior permission for “lawful transit through international waters.” Last month, a China Coast Guard vessel rammed a Philippine boat on a refueling mission near the same shoal, according to the Philippine Coast Guard. China blamed the collision on the Philippine side. China and the Philippines, which has a mutual defense treaty with the US, both contest sovereignty over Sabina Shoal and the entire Spratly Islands archipelago. PRATAS STANDOFF In a separate incident on Tuesday at the top end of the South China Sea, Taiwan’s Coast Guard said a Chinese Coast Guard ship had entered restricted waters near the Taiwan-controlled Pratas Islands. The Taiwan Coast Guard said its ship the “Taichung” was dispatched to warn away the Chinese boat, while both sides broadcast messages to each other. The Chinese ship broadcast that “the so-called Republic of China does not exist,” referring to Taiwan’s official name, while the Taiwanese ship broadcast back that “the Republic of China, Taiwan, is a sovereign and independent country,” Taiwan’s Coast Guard said, adding the standoff was continuing. China’s Taiwan Affairs Office did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The office said last week that Taiwan must “bear the consequences” of its Coast Guard using a water cannon against a Chinese fishing boat near the Pratas . The Pratas Islands lie roughly between southern Taiwan and Hong Kong, but are only lightly defended and security is the responsibility of Taiwan’s Coast Guard. China has also been stepping up coast guard activity around Taiwan, including off the island’s east coast, causing concern in Western capitals. China views democratically governed Taiwan as its own territory. Speaking at a forum in Taipei on Tuesday, the chair of a review commission appointed by the US Congress said Chinese coast guard patrols to the east of Taiwan were “highly destabilizing.” Addressing the same event, Taiwan’s National Security Council Secretary-General Joseph Wu said China had no legal claim to the waters off the island’s east. articles.title: FERC comes up with three-tiered fast track plan to streamline US LNG permitting
articles.summary: FERC has proposed an LNG blanket authorization program to slash red tape, optimize permitting, and fast-track U.S. energy infrastructure development.
articles.body: Authorities & Government October 20, 2026 · 15 hours ago FERC comes up with three-tiered fast track plan to streamline US LNG permitting FERC has proposed an LNG blanket authorization program to slash red tape, optimize permitting, and fast-track U.S. energy infrastructure development. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email LNG tanker (for illustration purposes) Source: U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) Aiming to cement U.S. energy dominance, the U.S. Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) has unveiled a historic proposal to create a three-tiered fast-track system for liquefied natural gas (LNG) projects, sparking a new era of regulatory certainty for developers by slashing years of case-by-case permitting delays. While announcing in a unanimous vote to accelerate LNG infrastructure development through a landmark blanket authorization program, the U.S. Federal Energy Regulatory Commission emphasized the proposal would streamline permitting, speed energy infrastructure development, and deliver unprecedented regulatory certainty for project developers. FERC’s notice of proposed rulemaking (NOPR) intends to establish an LNG blanket authorization program to allow eligible activities at LNG facilities to proceed without case-specific authorization orders under Sections 3 and 7 of the Natural Gas Act (NGA). This program is modeled on the commission’s 40-year blanket certificate program for interstate natural gas pipelines. Laura V. Swett , FERC’s Chairman, commented: “American energy dominance requires us to build and maintain the energy infrastructure our country needs without unnecessary delay. I am immensely proud of FERC’s historic proposal. “It shows what can be possible when we combine regulatory excellence, robust safeguards, and a firm commitment to the nation’s energy future. Consumers benefit when more energy infrastructure is online, dependable, and affordable, and FERC is helping make that future a reality.” Related Articles Fossil Energy FERC easing rules to expedite construction of natural gas projects 3 min read The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission is proposing a three-tiered authorization framework under which certain activities could proceed automatically, with periodic reporting, while others would require advance notice to FERC. Interested parties will have 60 days after the NOPR is published in the Federal Register to submit comments. Under the automatic authorization umbrella are activities that would not increase an LNG plant’s authorized capacity, expand the authorized vertical or horizontal extents within the plant’s footprint, or cause flows, levels, volumes, pressures, temperatures, compositions, or loads to exceed applicable design limits. A 60-day prior notice covers activities that may increase the plant’s authorized capacity but remain within the plant’s footprint and do not cause operating conditions to exceed the design limits of the affected or remaining facilities. A 90-day prior notice entails construction of new LNG facilities, such as liquefaction trains, LNG tanks, and marine berths, and related auxiliary systems, including those located outside the plant’s footprint, subject to limitations on facility type, location, and size. Related Articles Clean Fuel Would permitting reform get rid of the red tape for U.S. energy infrastructure projects? 6 min read In addition, FERC’s NOPR also proposes standard environmental and engineering design conditions to address the potential impacts of projects approved under the blanket authorization program, as well as other requirements to ensure compliance with all applicable laws. articles.summary: OceanAlpha has received Approval in Principle (AiP) from Bureau Veritas Marine & Offshore (BV) for the design of its L42B uncrewed surface vessel...
articles.body: Branded Content October 20, 2026 · 16 hours ago OceanAlpha L42B marine survey uncrewed surface vessel (USV) receives Bureau Veritas Approval in Principle (AiP) certificate Written in partnership with OceanAlpha 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email @OceanAlpha OceanAlpha has received Approval in Principle (AiP) from Bureau Veritas Marine & Offshore (BV) for the design of its L42B uncrewed surface vessel (USV), developed for offshore hydrographic and geophysical survey operations. Issued on 31 July 2026, the AiP followed a review of the vessel’s design and proposed operations against BV’s NI 641 guidelines for autonomous shipping. The assessment covered the L42B’s general arrangement, communications and control architecture, and defined operating scenarios. BV concluded that the proposed design did not conflict with the applicable rules within the scope of its review. The assessment considered harbour manoeuvring in complex traffic, including docking and undocking, as well as open-sea survey and transit. These scenarios involve continuous operator supervision and remote control from a shore-based control centre or a support vessel. The AiP applies to the defined operating conditions and includes technical recommendations for further development. @OceanAlpha The L42B is an 8.51-metre aluminium catamaran designed for marine survey missions. Its modular payload platform can accommodate multibeam echo sounders, side-scan sonars and magnetometers for seabed mapping, subsea pipeline surveys and environmental monitoring. Under still-water conditions at an operating speed of four knots, the vessel is designed for missions lasting up to eight days. Its stated maximum range is 1,500 kilometres. The vessel combines diesel generators, electric propulsion and lithium iron phosphate batteries. Multiple communication links support remotely supervised operations in coastal and offshore environments, enabling operators to monitor navigation and intervene when required. These capabilities are intended to increase deployment flexibility and help reduce personnel exposure during offshore survey activities. A certificate awarding ceremony was held on 16 October 2026, attended by Mr. Maciej Lepicki, Greater China Vice President of Bureau Veritas Marine & Offshore, and Mr. Pinestone Shi, General Manager of OceanAlpha. “Receiving AiP from Bureau Veritas is a remarkable milestone in the development of the L42B,” said Mr. Pinestone Shi, General Manager of OceanAlpha. “The independent review provides valuable technical feedback as we continue to refine the vessel’s design and remote-operation capabilities. Our focus remains on delivering reliable, practical USV products and solutions for marine survey customers worldwide.” About OceanAlpha Founded in 2010, OceanAlpha develops and manufactures uncrewed surface vessels and integrated solutions for hydrographic surveying, offshore operations, maritime security, water rescue and firefighting. The company combines vessel engineering, payload integration and remote-operation technologies to support customers across international marine markets.
